description: Canyon de Chelly (CACH) National Monument operates separate water systems for potable water needs inside the Park and the Park‚Äôs fire suppression systems. otable water for use inside the Park is supplied from a 120-foot drilled well located near the southwest corner of the parking lot for the Thunderbird lodge, with a backup potable water connection provided by the NTUA. A well with a submersible pump (normal operations 35 gallons/minute) supplies water to the distribution system. From the well, water travels through a depth filter to remove iron and then a carbon filter in series. Following filtration, a sodium hypochlorite solution is injected into the water. Through a liquid level control, potable water is pumped to a 100,000-gallon buried concrete potable water storage reservoir, comprised of two, 50,000-gallon compartments that are operated in series. This gravity reservoir is located on top of a hill, east of the Park‚Äôs maintenance facility. The south potable water reservoir was built during the 1980s and was identified as the settling reservoir. The north potable water reservoir was identified as the reservoir supplying the distribution system. From the two potable water storage reservoirs, potable water is distributed to service connections within the Park including the maintenance shop, the visitor center, park headquarters, the campground, and park housing.

Potable water is supplied to the south side of the Park through an 8-inch cast iron water main from the city of Coolidge, supplied by Arizona Water, a municipal water source. This water supply passes through a meter, located in a valve vault immediately southeast of the maintenance facility wall, and then passes through a 6-inch Wilkins 950 XL reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device prior to entering the Park property. An additional Wilkins 950 XL reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device is installed on the meter bypass, located adjacent to the 6-inch Wilkins 950 XL reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device. Potable water from Arizona Water supplies the Park Visitor Center, maintenance complex, VIP RV host site connections, and the garden area. Additionally, potable water is used for irrigation of the garden area, located on the north side of the property.

description: This non-community transient water system serves all the developed Park areas (Bonita campground, park headquarters, park housing, and visitor center) with the exception of Quarters 29. This system is served by a 116-foot drilled well, located inside the campground. This well was drilled during 1962. This drilled well delivers water at a rate of 40 gallons-per-minute. This well is cased with a 6-inch steel casing. The bottom 60 feet of this well is screed with a slotted PVC pipe, and the remainder of the hole is cased to the surface. A sanitary seal between the borehole and the conductor casing extends down 70 feet below grade. Gravel pack covers the whole length of the screen section. Water enters the treatment house through a 2-inch water line, is chlorinated using a sodium hypochlorite solution, and is sent for storage inside three, buried concrete potable water storage reservoirs. These three concrete potable water storage reservoirs have capacities of 10,000 gallons, 20,000 gallons, and 50,000 gallons and are connected in series (20,000 to 10,000 to 50,000). These potable water storage reservoirs are located on a hill above the Park‚Äôs developed area. Potable water is sent by gravity from these reservoirs to the Park‚Äôs distribution system.

This non-public groundwater system serves the Quarter 29 (Fischer House) residence. Water is pumped from a drilled well, located to the east of the Faraway Ranch house. Water is chlorinated inside a brown storage shed and sent to the house through a 2-inch water main. There is no potable water storage reservoir for this water system.

This transient, non-community water system serves the entire Park including the maintenance shop, Park headquarters, the Visitor Center, Park housing, and the campground. Water is pumped from a well drilled in 2008. Water from the well enters into a treatment building, located to the East of the well. Water passes through a meter and undergoes disinfection with a sodium hypochlorite solution. Treated water leaves the treatment building and is pumped to a 50,000-gallon above ground welded steel potable storage water reservoir, located above the hill, through a 2-inch PVC line. Treated water is distributed from the potable water storage reservoir throughout the Park utilizing a 6-inch transite pipe. During 2001, a microscopic particulate analysis (MPA) was conducted and identified a low probability of this system being under the influence of surface water.

This public transient non-community water system serves the entire Park, including the two park residences, the maintenance area, and the visitor center. Water is pumped from a 220-foot drilled well to a treatment building where it is disinfected with a liquid sodium hypochlorite solution. Treated water is pumped off of a timer to limit water production to nighttime (though this can be manually bypassed). Additionally, there is also a throttling valve inside the treatment building to control the rate at which water is pumped and minimize drawdown. Treated water is then pumped to an 870-gallon chlorine contact tank to achieve the calculated chlorine contact time. Treated water is either sent to distribution throughout the Park or pumped uphill to a 10,000-gallon above ground welded steel potable water storage reservoir. There is no return line installed on this water distribution system.

The visitor center water system consists of a drilled well, pumphouse (with water softener, small cartridge filter, and sodium hypochlorite injection for disinfection), 50,000 gallon welded steel water storage tank, and water distribution system.  The system serves a visitor center, offices, residences (4 houses and 4 apartment units), and a maintenance facility.  The supply and distribution lines in this area were replaced in 2008.

description: This transient, non-community water system serves the Lees Ferry area of the Park ‚Äì including the Park housing units, the comfort station at the boat dock, the campground, and the RV dump station. Water for this system is supplied through two intake pipes directly from intakes in the Colorado River. These two, buried intake pipes are operated by dual, 15-horsepower Baldor and Uniclosed pumps that can pump up to 50 GPM. Water drawn from the Colorado River is treated with aluminum sulfate (AlSO4) and a polymer through flash injection. This raw water travels through a mechanical flocculator, then to a tube settler, and finally a multimedia filter composed of anthracite, fine sand, course sand, and gravel. Following filtration, sodium hypochlorite solution is injected into the raw water. Potable water is treated through in an in-line ultra-violet (UV) system. Following ultra-violet treatment, potable water is stored inside a 2,5000 clear well for mixing and chlorine contact. Potable water is sent to an elevated, 150,000-gallon welded steel potable water storage reservoir for holding prior to distribution throughout the Lees Ferry area of the Park.

This community water system serves the Wahweap Area of the Park ‚Äì including the lodge, restaurant, Park housing, maintenance facility, campground, and boat docks. Historically, the source of this water for this water system was from two drilled wells, identified as Well # 3 and Well # 4. Well # 4 is a 360-foot-deep drilled well that is currently dry. Well # 3 is a 400-foot-deep well that is online and responsible for providing water for this water system; however, testing has revealed a high arsenic content in water procured from this drilled well. Water from well # 3 is pumped through a Franklin Electric submersible pump, model # 2391088504. Water enters the water treatment building were it is treated with gaseous chlorine. Chlorine gas is injected into the water utilizing Water Solutions using pump model CL # 1021089 at a pressure over 180 PSI. Following pH adjustment with chlorine dioxide gas, arsenic is removed from the water utilizing an AdEdge Water Technologies filtration system consisting of E33 media rated for up to 425 gallons-per-minute of flow. After potable water undergoes arsenic treatment through this filtration system, it is sent for storage inside three, 500,000-gallon above ground welded-steel potable water storage reservoirs prior to distribution. Liquid level inside these reservoirs is telemetry controlled. Pumps at Wells #3 and #4 are automatically started and stopped based on water levels in the potable water storage reservoirs.

water_system_name: South Rim Reclaimed Non-Potable Water System
description: Grand Canyon National Park has produced reclaim water since the 1920‚Äôs. It was originally used as water for steam locomotives. The modern reclaim water system routes wastewater plant effluent through two coagulation/flocculation tanks, a clarifying/settling tank, and two mixed media sand/gravel filters. A gas chlorination system adds 2ppm chlorine to the water before it feeds into a 150,000-gallon clear well located under the reclaim building. Reclaim water is pumped to two reclaim tanks, one located near the school (150,000 gallon) and one located near CVIP (125,000 gallon). The reclaim water is used primarily for flushing toilets and irrigating grassy areas in the park. When the reclaim water demand is less than the plant effluent flow, the reclaim water is routed through two 500 gallon sodium metabisulfite dechlorination tanks, through an effluent flow meter, and to three lagoons out on Raw Well Road. These lagoons were originally built in the 1930‚Äôs for wastewater treatment, but taken out of service after building the wastewater treatment plant. Water held in the lagoons is currently used for fire protection purposes. After the lagoons are full a valve located after the effluent flow meter can be turned to route water to an outfall that discharges into a small drywash. This water runs approximately 1 mile down the drywash before completely percolating into the ground.

description:
This water system serves a 300-site trailer village, Hemenway Harbor, Lake Mead Marina (755 slips), Las Vegas Marina at Hemenway Harbor(635 slips), an 89-site campground, a picnic area with two comfort stations, ranger station, administrative offices, Lake Mead Lodge motel with administrative offices, 110-passenger tour vessel with on-board restaurant, marina snack bar and administrative offices, staff housing, 15 VIP sites, RV dump stations, dry boat storage, native plant nursery, FHA and construction contractor trailers/offices, interagency boat dock, fish cleaning stations, fire station, rescue quarters, and maintenance facility. It consists of a connection to the Boulder City lateral from the Southern Nevada water system, a 300K gallon concrete water storage tank, and distribution piping. Water flows into the water storage tank through a service connection to the Southern Nevada water system. The connection is equipped with a reduced pressure backflow preventer that is maintained by the City. An altitude valve that opens and closes to allow a four-foot drawdown in the tank controls water level in the tank. 
The water service connection to the Las Vegas Boat Harbor at Hemenway consists of a 3-inch pvc line that runs below grade to the top of the boat ramp where it transitions to a covered concrete channel that runs the length of the ramp. At lake level the pvc line transitions to a hose that joins the line to the water line that runs under the dock to the marina. The Desert Princess dock is connected to the Boulder City water system.

The water system serves a 3-loop RV campground and dump station, five comfort stations, marina snack bar, administrative offices, yacht club, trailer park, NPS staff and concessions employee housing, maintenance building, fire station, and a fish cleaning station. It consists of a raw water intake in Lake Mead, two intake pumps and water transmission line, a 500,000-gallon concrete raw water storage tank, a water treatment plant, a 100,000-gallon welded steel and a 300,000-gallon welded steel finished water storage tank, and a distribution system consisting of 6-inch and 8-inch PVC pipe. Raw water is pumped from the lake by the intake pump located on a floating barge to the raw water storage tank. A pressure transducer in the raw water tank controls this pump. Water flows by gravity to the treatment plant. Water treatment consists of filtration and disinfection and a disinfection byproduct {TTHM) removal system. Turbidity is continually monitored in the raw water and both turbidity and chlorine residual are continually monitored in the product water. The raw water is first pumped through a microfiltration system where particles down to 0.2 microns are removed. The filtered water discharges to a clearwell. It is then pumped through a 5-micron pre-filter followed by a nanofiltration system. The nanofilter is currently not in operation. The filtration system produces 181 gpm of treated water. The filtered water is disinfected using chlorine before being discharged to the final clearwell. This clearwell provides contact time for disinfection. Backwash water can either be discharged to a drainage ditch outside the treatment building (as permitted by NDEP), or it can be diverted to the sanitary sewer. The treated water is then pumped to the finished water storage tanks via a dedicated fill line before entering the distribution system.

description: The water system serves an RV campground, trailer village, marina store, trailer park, two campgrounds each with two comfort stations, ranger station, administrative offices, NPS employee housing, and NPS maintenance shop. It consists of a raw water intake in Lake Mead, intake pumps and water transmission line, a raw water storage tank, a water treatment plant, a 500,000-gallon above-grade concrete treated water storage tank, and a 2-compartment 145,000-gallon concrete water storage tank (only compartment 2 being used). Two intake pumps located on a floating barge pump water from the lake to the raw water storage tank. This tank has three separate compartments. One compartment is used for irrigation storage. Water in the other two compartments is raw water. A pressure transducer in the raw water tank controls the intake pump. Water flows by gravity to the treatment plant. Water treatment consists of filtration and disinfection. The raw water is first pumped through a microfiltration system, which removes particles down to 0.2 microns. The filtered water discharges to a clearwell. It is then pumped through a 5-micron pre-filter followed by a nanofiltration system. The nanofilter is currently not in operation. The filtration system produces 180 gpm of treated water. The filtered water is disinfected using chlorine before being discharged to the final clearwell, which provides contact time for disinfection. The treated water is then pumped to the water storage tank via a dedicated fill line. The backwash water is discharged to a lined pit outside the water treatment plant. The pit removes any solids and dissipates energy before the clarified water is overflows to the ground (as permitted by NDEP). The distribution system consists of two pressure zones. A booster pump (2) delivers water from the 500,000-gallon treated water storage tank to the 145,000-gallon water storage tank above the 120-site RV park and provides water to the RV park.

description: The water system serves the marina (824 slips), marina store, motel, restaurant, a fish cleaning station, ranger station, maintenance yard, NPS and concessions staff housing, boat repair shop and storage yard, trailer village and campground. It consists of a raw water intake in Lake Mojave, two intake pumps and water transmission line, a water treatment plant, a 500,000-gallon above-grade welded steel water storage tank (A-tank out of service) and a 500,000-gallon above-grade concrete water tank, and distribution system. The intake pumps located on a floating barge pump draw water from the lake and pump it to the treatment plant. The plant contains four clearwells located below the plant floor, a microfiltration system, a nanofiltration system, chlorine disinfection system. Before treatment, Acid Magic is added to lower the pH {~8.3 to 7.3) due to the mussels and a caustic is added after to raise the pH. One clearwell is used for irrigation storage, and one provides raw water to the microfiltration unit. The other compartments are treated for potable use. Water treatment consists of filtration and disinfection. The raw water is pumped through a microfiltration system that removes particles down to 0.2 microns. The filtered water discharges to a clearwell. The system is then designed to pump the water through a 1 micron pre-filter followed by a nanofiltration system. However, the nanofilter is currently not in operation since the microfilter treated water meets current MCLs. The filtration system produces about 450,000 gallons per day, or about 330 gpm, of treated water. The filtered water is disinfected chlorine solution before being discharged to the final clearwell, which provides contact time for disinfection. The treated water is then pumped to the water storage tanks via a dedicated fill line. The backwash water can be used for irrigation or discharged to the sanitary sewer. This discharge is permitted under NPDES. The distribution system consists of a 10-inch pvc pipe from the water treatment plant to the water storage tanks, and 4, 6, and 8-inch PVC pipe serving the remaining facilities. A radio telemetry (SCADA) system signals water level in the storage tanks to the treatment plant to fill the tanks. Turbidity is continually monitored in the raw water, and both turbidity and chlorine residual are continually monitored in the product water.

The water system serves a 42-space RV campground, marina store and restrooms, employee housing, trailer park and a fish cleaning station. It consists of a raw water intake in Lake Mead, two intake pumps and water transmission line, a concrete above grade raw water storage tank, a water treatment plant, a 150,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank and a 150,000-gallon concrete finished water storage tank, and a distribution system consisting of 6-inch and 8-inch PVC pipe. Raw water is pumped from the lake by 2 intake pumps located on a floating barge to the raw water storage tank. A pressure transducer in the raw water tank controls these pumps. Water flows by gravity to the treatment plant. Water treatment consists of filtration and disinfection. The raw water is first pumped through a microfiltration system where particles down to 0.2 microns are removed. The filtered water discharges to a clearwell. It is then pumped through a 5-micron pre-filter followed by a nanofiltration system. The nanofilters are not in operation. The filtration system produces 181 gpm of treated water. The filtered water is disinfected using calcium hypochlorite before being discharged to the final clearwell. This clearwell provides contact time for disinfection. Backwash water is discharged (as permitted by NDEP) to a drainage ditch outside the treatment building. The treated water is then pumped to a 150,000-gallon above grade concrete water storage tank and a 150,000-gallon above grade welded steel water storage tank via a dedicated fill line before entering the distribution system.

description: The water system serves the marina (95 slips existing, 695 authorized), marina store, restaurant and bar, overnight cabins, administrative offices, commercial ice making facility, a fish cleaning station, ranger station, maintenance yard, campground, RV dump station and concessioner and NPS staff housing. description: This transient, non-community water system serves the Visitor Center, Visitor Center comfort station, one Park housing unit with 3 single bedroom apartments, an additional Park housing unit, and one Park office building. The source for this water system is an approximately 160-foot deep drilled well, located inside a well house in the Park housing area. Water is pumped from this well through a submersible pump. Water enters into the pumphouse, passes through a meter, and is then injected with a liquid sodium hypochlorite solution. Following injection, potable water passes through a 2-inch Watts 600 W06 reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device prior to distribution to the park housing units, park office space, visitor center, and visitor center through a 6-inch water main. Additionally, potable water is stored inside a 50,00-gallon welded-steel potable water storage reservoir, located uphill to the north of the Park visitor center. There is not a separate transmission line to the 50,000-gallon welded steel potable water storage reservoir; the distribution system serves as a transmission line to the reservoir.

description: This transient, non-community water system serves the entire Montezuma Well area of the Park. This includes the maintenance shop, the two Mission-66 Park residence units, and a comfort station with a men‚Äôs restroom and a women‚Äôs restroom. The source for this water system is an approximately 160-foot deep drilled well, located inside a water treatment building. Water is pumped from this well through a submersible pump. Water enters into the pumphouse, passes through a meter and then the potable water line splits into two 1.5-inch metal distribution lines ‚Äì one, 1.5-inch line serving the maintenance shop and one, 1.5-inch line serving the two Park residence units. Water delivered through each of these lines passes through a flow switch prior to treatment. Each of these lines is then injected with a liquid sodium hypochlorite solution. Following treatment, water from each line is pressurized through a 125 PSI Goulds HydroPro pressure tanks and then the water lines exit outside of the treatment building. To achieve appropriate chlorine contact, each 1.5-inch metal water line increases into 8-inch pipes ‚Äì providing approximately 600 gallons of mixing capability per each line. These two separate water lines enter back into the pumphouse. One of these distribution lines provides potable water to the two Mission 66 housing units, while the other distribution line serves the maintenance shop.

description: This public, non-transient non-community water system provides all the water for this Park. This system serves the maintenance shop, the campground comfort station, employee housing, and the visitor center. Water is pumped from an 870-foot drilled well (identified as well # 4) with a submersible pump (Stenner Model 85MHP40), which is designed to pump 15 gallons per minute. Water is pumped into the pumphouse where it undergoes treatment with a sodium hypochlorite solution.  Water is sent to a 100,000-gallon, above ground welded steel storage reservoir for storage. This reservoir was built during 1973 at a diameter of 33 feet and a height of 15 feet. From the above ground welded steel storage reservoir, water is pumped to a booster station through two Balor-Reliance (model 85700817) booster pumps. Prior to distribution, water travels through a 200-gallon steel pressure tank (Wessels Company) at approximately 50-PSI prior to distribution.

The Parkwide water system serves all facilities in the Park including the Visitor Center, administrative offices, restrooms, maintenance area, residential area containing 20 houses and 10 VIP RV sites, a 208 site campground, resource management building, and visitor and resource protection building.

Water is pumped from two drilled wells ‚Äì well # 4 (or the south well) and well # 6 (or the north well) Well # 4, or the south well, was drilled during 1957 and is equipped with a submersible pump. A large, five-foot by five-foot square concrete apron surrounds the wellhead. Well # 6, or the north well, was rehabilitated during 2019 with the addition of a new submersible pump. A large, three-foot by three-foot square concrete apron surrounds the wellhead. The wellhead is enclosed inside a green cylinder attached to the square concrete apron that is secured with a lock. Potable water from these two tells enters the pumphouse, where it is treated through an automatic sodium hypochlorite injection system. Potable water from the pumphouse is pumped to a 100,000-gallon above ground potable water storage reservoir. The well pumps are controlled with an automatic reservoir level control system. Potable water is then transferred by gravity to either the 50,000 gallon above ground potable water reservoir that services the campground, or direct distribution to the Visitor Center, administrative, maintenance, and housing areas. Potable water enters the distribution system through a 6-inch asbestos cement (AC) water. Flow to the 50,000 gallon above ground potable water reservoir is controlled by a float valve.  The 50,000 gallon above ground potable water reservoir services the campground distribution system and an employee duplex. A 4-inch PVDF bypass line is present if needed so that either tank can be taken offline.

The NPS operates the Transient Non-Community Water System on tribal lands.  Water system PWSID# is for a Tribal System (Kaibab Band of Paiute Tribe has primacy).  The well is located approximately 2 miles north of the visitor center.  The well is a 230 foot deep drilled well with a submersible pump.  The water after being pumped goes through a well house where it is injected with liquid sodium hypochlorite then transferred to a 500,000 gallon buried concrete storage tank through HDPE lines.  The storage tank has custom made tamper proof lids.  The water line does have connections to the tribal water system that are fitted with RPZ backflow preventers to prevent backflow into the NPS lines.

Backflow preventers are tested annually by a contractor that checks the fire sprinkler system.

The Manning Camp Water System is a non-public water system that serves the cabin at Manning Camp, located on Mica Mountain at approximately 8,000 feet of elevation. No potable water serves this cabin and water is only provided when there is a demand for water (e.g., firefighting or trail work). Use of Manning Camp is seasonal, with an operation period typically from late March to mid-November. The water source at Manning Camp is a natural spring. There is a 15-foot-deep hole that is a reliable source of water during the drier months. Water is pumped from the source into a small concrete box with percolation holes to trap organic matter. After passing through the percolation holes, spring water enters the pumphouse where it first passes through a 50-micron filter, then a 5 micron filter, and finally through a 1-micron absolute filter in series. Following filtration, filtered spring water is pumped to an above-ground 2,600-gallon plastic potable water storage tank. There is a spigot next to this non-potable water storage tank that will drain the contents inside this storage reservoir. Non-potable water is then gravity fed to a cabin for staff use only. A spigot is provided next to the cabin for staff use. Additionally, a rain catchment cistern is provided adjacent to the cabin spigot to collect non-potable rainwater for additional water supply. Staff stated this water is not used for culinary, drinking, or hygienic purposes. This rainwater catchment cistern is not connected to the spring water source.

This transient, non-community water system serves the Tucson Mountain District (West District) of the Park. The well providing water for the Tucson Mountain District water system is a 660-feet drilled well. The submersible pump, Goulds model no. 10GS50 is located approximately 600 feet below this surface, and pumps at a rate of approximately 16 gallons per minute. The wellhead is located in an enclosed locking structure to the northeast of the water treatment room. A four foot by four foot concrete apron surrounds the well. The enclosed metal structure housing the wellhead is secured with two locks. Water from the drilled well enters through a meter, passes through a check valve, undergoes treatment using liquid sodium hypochlorite, and then is sent to distribution through a 6-inch main line which decreases to 3 inches at the inlet of the 50,000-gallon underground potable water reservoir. Water is then distributed throughout the Park using a 3-inch PVC line. This water system serves the Red Mountain Visitor Center, comfort station at the Visitor Center, Operations Building, Education Building, living quarters 31, and living quarters 32.

The water system at the Monument serves the visitor center, residences, maintenance shop, the Crater Comfort Station, and the Bonito Forest Service campground located across the road from the visitor center.

Water for the Monument is purchased from the Doney Park Water Company.  The facility is classified as a distribution system which requires a minimum of two bacteriological water samples monthly. The Doney Park Water Company does not chlorinate the water, which is acceptable under the Regulations of the Arizona State Department of Environmental Quality.  The staff at the Monument installed a hypochlorinator at the base of the reservoir.  Chlorination provides residual protection for any future contamination. Water for Sunset Crater is obtained by pumping water each evening from a pumping station located at Doney Park through the 2.5 miles of water line.  The pumping is started by a time clock.  An automatic chlorinator adds chlorine.  There is no automatic control; a valve is opened at the inlet of the system before Doney Water begins pumping.  The reservoir is a 50,000 gallon, 100-foot elevated steel tank that was erected in 1965.  The chlorinator is located in a building constructed at the base of the water tower.

The park used to have its own public water system (AZ0403715), but this system was taken offline in 1977.

This transient, non-community water system serves all the facilities in the Park including the Visitor Center, the picnic area comfort station, the Park headquarters building, the four Park housing units, and the Park maintenance buildings. The source of water is from a well drilled during 1963 (ID # 55-629108). This well is drilled to a depth of 140 feet at a diameter of 6 inches. This 6-inch casing is torch perforated from a depth of 30 feet to the bottom of the 140-foot drilled well. A sanitary seal is installed to a depth of 5 feet. Water is pumped from the well, located inside the water treatment house, through a submersible pump. Water undergoes a softening process utilizing a Advanced Water Systems water softening, installed in 2000, and is then treated with a sodium hypochlorite solution. Potable water is sent to a 50,000-gallon buried concrete potable water storage reservoir. Potable water flows by gravity to the picnic area comfort station, the maintenance buildings, and the four Park housing units. A booster pump inside the pumphouse lifts water from this 50,000-gallon buried concrete potable water reservoir to a 25,000-gallon above ground welded-steel potable water storage reservoir located uphill from the visitor center. Float switches inside the buried concrete potable water storage reservoir control the submersible well pump. A float switch inside the 25,000-gallon above ground welded-steel potable water storage reservoir.

The distribution system consists of 1.25-inch galvanized pipe, 4- and 6-inch asbestos cement (AC) pipe, and 2-inch schedule 80 PVC pipe.  Four-inch AC pipe runs from the 50,000-gallon storage tank to the picnic area comfort station, maintenance area, and residential area.  A 4-inch PVC line runs from the transfer pump located in the pumphouse to the visitor center parking lot.  A 6 inch AC line connects the 25,000 gallon storage tank to the distribution system

description: This non-public water system serves the Maintenance/Administrative (South) side of the Park including: the maintenance complex (fire suppression system, four hose bibs, one toilet, one restroom sink, and one eye wash), the casita (kitchen sink, one toilet, one restroom sink, and a bathtub), and the administrative office (fire suppression system, one breakroom sink, one toilet, and one restroom sink). Water is supplied from a 138 foot deep drilled well with a static water level of 13 feet. A submersible pump with a capacity of 70 gallons-per-minute (5 horsepower) supplies the well. Water is then treated with a sodium hypochlorite solution and pressurized through a 1,000-gallon pressure tank, located adjacent to the wellhead. Potable water is then sent to either storage inside an above ground, plastic, 1,800-gallon potable water storage reservoir; or sent for storage for fire suppression. Following storage inside the 1,800-gallon potable water storage reservoir, water is sent for distribution. All potable water for fire suppression passes through a Febco LF825Y reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device and is then pumped using a diesel motor to a 50,000-gallon, above ground welded steel potable water storage reservoir for fire suppression.

This transient non-community (TNC) water system serves the Mission/Visitor Center (North) side of the Park including: the Visitor Center (kitchen sink, three restrooms) and the Boundy House residence (kitchen sink, one toilet, one restroom sink, and a shower). Water is supplied from a 125 foot deep drilled well with a static water level of 13 feet. This well is identified as well # 1. A submersible pump set at 60 feet with a capacity of 12 gallons-per-minute (0.5 horsepower) supplies the well. Water is then treated with a sodium hypochlorite solution utilizing a Pulsatron A-Plus series injection pump. Following chlorination, the potable water line splits. One line is pumped through Pump # 1 to an Well-X-Trol Amtrol 100 PSI pressure tank. The other line is pumped through Pump # 2 to an Well-X-Trol Amtrol 100 PSI pressure tank. Potable water from this line passes through a Febco 825YA reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device prior to it‚Äôs storage inside a 50,000 underground, concrete potable water storage reservoir where it is held for distribution. Potable water is distributed through the Mission/Visitor Center (North) side of the Park through 6-inch PVC main lines and HDPE service line piping.

This transient, non-community water system serves the entire Tuzigoot National Monument. This includes the Visitor Center; comfort station with a men‚Äôs restroom, women‚Äôs restroom, and custodial closet; the maintenance shop; the Park irrigation system; and the two Park housing units. The source of this water system is an approximately 160-feet deep, 6-inch drilled well located inside the water treatment building, located underneath the visitor center. Water is pumped from this well through two, high-frequency submersible pumps. Each pump is equipped with a 5 horsepower Baldor motor. Water is pumped into a water treatment building, where it first passes through a meter and is then injected with a liquid sodium hypochlorite solution for disinfection. Potable water is pumped into the adjacent water pressurization building where it is pressurized utilizing a NAT‚ÄôL BD bladderless pressure tank, with a maximum pressure of 80 PSI. Pressure switches control the operation of the booster pumps. Following pressurization, the potable water line splits with one AC and ductile iron line supplying the fire suppression system; while the other AC and ductile iron line provides potable water to the 50,000-gallon below-ground concrete potable water storage reservoir. A Watts 2000B ¬æ-inch reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device is installed on the potable water line supplying the fire suppression system. The liquid level inside the 50,000-gallon below-ground potable water storage reservoir is controlled through a float system.

The water system is classified as a public transient non-community system. All of the facilities at the Monument (eight service connections) are served by the water system.

Water is obtained from a drilled well approximately 1,800 feet deep, located in a well house approximately 200 feet from the visitor center.  A minimum of two samples are required per month. 
 
Water is chlorinated via a hypochlorinator (12.5% liquid sodium hypochlorite) that is located in the pumphouse.  The water is pumped to a 55,000-gallon steel reservoir, which is a 100-foot elevated steel tank erected in 1961.  Some new distribution lines were installed in 2010.

All of the facilities at the Monument, except the Doney Picnic Area, are served by a single water system.  No water is provided at the picnic area.  The facility is classified as a Public Transient Non-Community Water System.  Water is obtained from a drilled well, approximately 905 feet deep, located near the maintenance shop. The water is routinely sampled twice a month for bacteriological quality.  
Reverse osmosis (RO) units and water softeners are located in each residence to improve the aesthetic qualities of the water for drinking and cooking. The water is chlorinated with a premixed hypochlorite solution in the pumphouse. The free residual of the chlorine is tested daily.

The water is pumped through a four-inch PolyVinyl Chloride (PVC) line to two glass coated, bolted-steel, reservoirs on the hill above the visitor center.  One of the reservoirs is a 57,000-gallon reservoir, the other is a 52,000-gallon reservoir. The reservoirs are piped and valved to permit either parallel or series operation. The reservoirs are normally drained through the six-inch Asbestos Cement (AC) distribution line.

This system serves the Scorpion developed area of East Santa Cruz Island. Facilities include a Visitor Center, historic residence, two campgrounds, NPS housing area (2 permanent staff) and the maintenance facility. Scorpions is visited by numerous day use visitors and campers. The system consists of a 55' well, sodium hypochlorite injection and 3 poly storage tanks. There is no grid power here, all electrical needs are handled by photovoltaic arrays.

description: Facilities on San Miguel Island consist of a single structure housing a ranger station, two 1-bedroom apartments, and a bunkhouse, and a visitor campground.  Water is provided only to the ranger station/residence.  The water system consists of a shallow well, a 500-gallon polyethylene water tank with submersible booster pump, a dedicated 1 ¬º inch pvc dedicated fill line to an 8,000-gallon and a 6,000-gallon buried fiberglass water storage tank, and 1 ¬º inch pvc distribution piping.  The submersible well pump is set to energize on a timer, depending on the water level in the intermediate 500-gallon tank.  When the timer calls for water, if the float switch in the 500-gallon tank is in the on (down) position, the well pump delivers water to the 500-gallon tank until either the timer or float switch de-energizes it.  When the water in the 500-gallon tank reaches booster "pump on" level, the float switch energizes the booster pump which delivers water to the fiberglass water storage tanks via a dedicated fill line.  A water meter records the volume of water delivered from the well to the water storage tanks.  The fiberglass tanks are valved such that the 8,000-gallon tank supplies sinks and the 6,000-gallon tank supplies the toilets.  Each tank has separate overflow and drain lines.  Water flows out of each tank by separate outlets to the ranger station.  Valving at the station controls from which tank water is drawn.  Water is drawn from one tank at a time.  The two outlet lines join downstream from the valves before passing through a second water meter and entering the building.

This year-round system serves a 50-house park residential area, maintenance facility, elementary school, and swimming pool.  It consists of a warm water spring, a weir box, a treatment building containing a 1 micron absolute pre-filter, a reverse osmosis filtration (RO), a hypochlorinator for injection of sodium hypochlorite solution, a 350,000-gallon in ground concrete water tank, and distribution system.

Spring water flows by gravity to the weir box.  Piping and pressure reducing valves in the weir box direct the flow to either the water treatment building or to the irrigation system, depending on upstream pressure.  At the treatment building water first flows through the pre-filters followed by the RO filter.  Following the 5 micron and then 1 micron absolute filters, a portion of the water bypasses the RO filter and is used to blend with the RO treated water to reduce the corrosiveness of the filtrate.  The filtrate is chlorinated with sodium hypochlorite solution before it discharges into the water tank.  Filter concentrate and backwash water discharge to the sewer system.  The treated water then enters the distribution system to the NPS housing.

This year-round system serves a comfort station with a drinking fountain and a hose bibb, and hose bibbs in a small campground.  It consists of water from a spring that flows by gravity through about five miles of 1¬º-inch water line to a 20,000-gallon underground concrete water storage reservoir.  The water flows through a tablet hypochlorinator that uses calcium hypochlorite before entering the tank.  Water is then fed by gravity from the tank to the facilities.

This year-round system serves the privately owned Furnace Creek Ranch and the Furnace Creek Inn, three NPS campgrounds (Furnace Creek, Texas Springs and Sunset) with 2,000 campsites, the NPS administrative complex, visitor center, and the Timbisha Indian Reservation.  It consists three wells, a 2-million gallon buried concrete water storage reservoir, a treatment building containing filtration and disinfection equipment, and a distribution system.  

When water in the 2-MG tanks reaches pump on level, a pump in one of the wells is called and pumps water at a rate of 325 gpm to the treatment building.  One additional well may be called depending on the water level in the water storage tank.  In the treatment building the water passes through two 1-micron filters then through reverse osmosis membrane filters.  Sodium hypochlorite solution is then injected before entering the 2-MG tank.  The 2-MG water tank provides water by gravity through a 10-inch water line to the privately owned Furnace Creek Ranch and Furnace Creek Inn,  the comfort stations and hose bibbs in the campgrounds, other park facilities, and the Timbisha Indian Reservation.  A SCADA control system allows the operator to monitor and control water treatment plant functions either at the plant or from a remote location.

description:
This year-round system serves the NPS maintenance yard, ranger station, six mobile homes, seven RV sites, and four apartments.  It consists of a spring collection box, chlorination building, and a two-compartment 100,000-gallon buried concrete water storage tank.  

Water flows by gravity from the spring box through a 6-inch AC pipe to the treatment building where the raw water first passes through a 5 micron and 1 micron filters followed by a Superior Vacufeed which injects sodium hypochlorite solution for disinfection.  The treated water then flows by gravity to the reservoirs, which provide storage and chlorine contact time.  A float valve controls flow into the tank.  It then flows into the distribution system.

This year-round system serves Scotty‚Äôs Castle, 11 residences, and a comfort station.  It consists of a spring collection building, a treatment building, a 60,000-gallon above-grade concrete water storage tank and a 40,000-gallon above-grade concrete water storage tank, and a distribution system.  

Spring water flows by gravity from the spring collection building to the water treatment building where a hypochlorinator injects sodium hypochlorite solution for disinfection.  The treated water flows into the storage tanks, which provide both storage and chlorine contact volume.  Flow into the tanks is controlled by altitude valves.  Water then flows by gravity out to the distribution system.  

-  Fluoride levels in the water (2.1 mg/l) exceed the State MCL (2.0 mg/l).  A waiver from the State requirement to treat the water for fluoride levels greater than the MCL (2.0 mg/l) has been requested.

This year-round system serves three unoccupied residences and a 17-site campground with three hose bibbs.  It consists of a spring that flows by gravity to a 10,000-gallon fiberglass water storage reservoir, and a chlorine tablet feeder for disinfection.  Treated water flows by gravity through the distribution system to the facilities.

This system consists of a 50-foot deep, 6-inch diameter drilled well, two 5000 gallon concrete storage tanks, and water distribution piping.  Water is pumped from the well by a submersible pump via a dedicated fill line to the water tank.  A metering pump is energized with the well pump to inject sodium hypochlorite into the fill line to the tank.  Free chlorine residuals are monitored and recorded daily.

This non-public system serves the maintenance building facilities including an employee restroom, a break room, shower, and several hose bibbs.  The system includes a 45-foot deep, 6-inch diameter drilled well with submersible pump and 20-gallon hydropneumatic tank housed in the pumphouse (for hose bibs only).  Inside the maintenance building there is the following equipment: a water softener, carbon filtration, an additional pressure tank (for potable water in the building), a holding tank.  There system currently is not treated and posted "Non-Potable" at all points of distribution.

Water is pumped from the well by the submersible pump through the treatment building before entering the maintenance building.  The storage tank provides storage volume and chlorine contact time, if needed.  The submersible pump is controlled by a pressure switch located adjacent to the pressure tanks.  When system pressure reaches 30 psi, the well pump energizes, pumping water at 7 gallons per minute.  The pump de-energizes when system pressure reaches 50 psi.

description: This year-round system serves a maintenance shop, visitor center, seasonal quarters, ranger quarters, fire dorm, and a campground with three comfort stations.  It consists of a pumphouse containing two booster pumps and a hypochlorinator, a 74,000-gallon fiberglass-lined, bolted steel water storage tank, and distribution system.  The water system is connected to the High Desert Water District municipal system.  Water flows into the pumphouse where the booster pumps pressurize the distribution system.  The pumping rate for each pump is about 60 gpm.  Sodium hypochlorite solution can be added before it leaves the pumphouse to boost chlorine residual of the incoming water.  It flows into the distribution system and to the water storage tank.  There is no dedicated fill line to the water storage tank.  The booster pumps are manually operated to fill the water tank.  The automatic timer control is not used.  At pump-off level, a signal is sent from the water tank to the well pump to de-energize.  The distribution system consists of 4-inch AC and 6-inch PVC water main.  There is an RV dump station at the campground.  The campground sites are served with frost-free hydrants located at various points throughout the campground.

This year-round Transient Non-Community (TNC) system serves the NPS maintenance yard, visitor center, seasonal quarters (3 houses and 2 duplexes), and a campground with four comfort stations.  It consists of a drilled well with a solar-powered submersible pump, a pumphouse containing a hypochlorinator and back-up generator, a 100,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank, and a distribution system.  The well, installed in November 1999, is 405 feet deep, has a 6-5/8 inch diameter PVC casing and a sanitary seal to 100 feet, and yields 26 gpm.  The pump is a 5 hp submersible solar-powered pump set at 375 feet below ground surface with pumping rate of 26 gpm at the system dynamic head.  The SCADA control system, installed in 2001, is located in the maintenance building.  It was designed to monitor and control pumping conditions, water storage tank water level, etc. from a central location.  It currently is not operational.  The system is operated  manually.  When the water level reaches 8 feet, the operator will energize the well pump, which also energizes the hypochlorinator to inject sodium hypochlorite solution.  The water is then pumped through about three miles of 4-inch AC pipe to the main distribution system.  This transmission line provides adequate contact time for chlorine disinfection.  A 6-inch pvc water line was installed from the visitor center to the water storage tank.  The well pump operates under solar power when available, and uses the back-up propane fueled generator when necessary.  The distribution system consists of 3-inch AC and 6-inch PVC water main.  There is an RV dump station at the campground.

This water system serves the visitor center (constructed 2003), two campground comfort stations, VIP trailer area, park administrative buildings, maintenance compound, and staff housing areas (six houses, one duplex, eight apartments).  It consists of a 823 foot drilled well (constructed in 2007), an 80 gpm submersible pump, continuous chlorination, and a 100,000-gallon underground concrete water storage reservoir. A 25 horsepower submersible well pump pumps water through the pumphouse where disinfection with liquid sodium hypochlorite occurs.  The treated water flows to the water storage tank via a 4-inch ductile iron dedicated fill line.   The treated water flows by gravity via 8 and 6-inch ductile iron pipes to the park facilities. This system collects 2 bacteriological samples per month of operation.

description: This seasonal system serves a 3-bedroom ranger residence and consists of a 330-ft deep drilled well, a pumphouse containing disinfection equipment, a 1,200-gallon elevated water storage tank, and distribution piping.  A propane generator provides power to the well pump and chlorinator equipment.  The system is manually operated.   Water pumped from the well is first disinfected then discharges via a dedicated fill line into a 1,200-gallon elevated storage tank.  Water is then fed by gravity to the ranger station.

This system serves an 86-site campground and ranger station.  Facilities include a uptake structure that extends into Butte Lake, a submersible booster pump and dedicated 4-inch PVC transmission line to the water treatment plant, a package treatment plant, a 40,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank, and water distribution system with 4 and 6-inch cast iron piping.  The system is operated manually.  The submersible pump lifts water at 50 gpm from the lake through the transmission line to the treatment plant.  Alum and polymer are added to the raw water before entering the treatment unit.  The filter is backwashed about once per week.  Sodium hypochlorite is injected in the filtered water and is then pumped to the water storage tank.  Chlorine residuals are monitored continuously in the water treatment plant and grab samples are taken daily throughout the campground.  Both raw water and treated water turbidities are continuously monitored in the treatment building.

This seasonal system has a groundwater spring source that does not require filtration.  The system provides water to Drakesbad Lodge, swimming pool, and Warner Valley campground.  It consists of a spring source, treatment building with a photovoltaic powered hypochlorinator, an aboveground, and a 40,000-gallon steel water storage tank Water flows by gravity from the spring (yield about 160 gpm) to the treatment building where sodium hypochlorite solution is added.  Disinfected water discharges into the water tank for contact time and storage.  It is then fed from the tank to the distribution system by gravity.

This seasonal system is a surface source that provides water for drinking fountains and hose bibbs in the campground.  Perforated pipes in the streambed collect the water that flows through roughing filters to remove some turbidity.  The water then flows to a treatment building where it flows through a bag filtration system consisting of a roughing filter, Giardia Filter, and Crypto filter, and is disinfected with liquid sodium hypochlorite, which is added by a proportional flow hypochlorinator.  The water then flows to a 10,000-gallon above ground steel storage tank.  The entire system operates on gravity.

This year round system serves the campground, the concession facilities, the maintenance facility, summer employee housing, and the information center.  It consists of  stream  infiltration gallery, a welded steel above-ground 100,000-gallon storage tank (summer), a 10,000-gallon glass lined bolted steel tank (winter), summer treatment building containing two multi-media pressure filters and chlorination equipment, winter treatment building containing a Rosedale 3-bag filtration system and chlorination equipment, and distribution piping.  The infiltration is backwashed weekly.  The filters are replaced when the pressure differential reaches 10 psi, or after one week, whichever occurs first.

Summer Operation:  Surface water flows from the intake structure by gravity to the treatment building where a small pump is used to force the water through two pressure filters and into the storage tank.  Coagulant is added upstream of the filters to aid filtration.  The water is chlorinated and stored in the 100,000-gallon storage tank next to the treatment building.  A second pump is used to backwash the filters.  The backwash water flows to a pond next to the treatment building where it evaporates.  Treated water flows by gravity into the distribution system.

Winter Operation:  A small capacity bag filter system (8 gpm) provides water during the winter.  Surface water bypasses the main treatment building but feeds the main storage tank.  From the tank it flows by gravity to another treatment building where it flows through three bag filters (roughing, Giardia, and Cryptosporidium) in series and is chlorinated with sodium hypochlorite solution.  It is then stored in a 10,000-gallon bolted, glass-lined steel tank for distribution to the system.  The bag filters are periodically changed.  The rinse-to-waste water is discharged to an adjacent leachfield.

This year round public community (PC) system serves 42 administrative and residential structures.  It consists of an intake structure, a 1,000-gallon sedimentation vault, treatment building with membrane filtration system and hypochlorinator, a 100,000-gallon buried concrete water storage tank, and a distribution system.  The entire system operates by gravity.  Flow is initiated when the low water level electrode energizes the water tank inlet valve to open and is stopped when the high water level electrode in the water tank closes the inlet valve.  Water flows from the intake structure to the treatment building where it flows  through two the membrane filters.  The water is chlorinated before flowing to a 100,000-gallon underground concrete storage tank.  The storage tank is divided into two 50,000-gallon sections, one for domestic use and the other for fire protection.  Water flows into the fire protection side and then overflows to the water supply side of the tank.  Opening a gate valve when needed accesses the fire protection side of the tank.  An old distribution system delivers the water to the points of use.

This year round system serves a 25-site campground, the Visitor Center, and entrance station.  The water system includes a source water infiltration gallery, a treatment building containing a mixed media pressure filter and treatment chemicals, a 40,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank, and distribution system piping.  The system is supplied from several streams and is operated year round.  The stream water collected by the infiltration gallery flows to the treatment building where it is first treated with caustic soda to raise pH and a coagulant, and then filtered to remove high levels of aluminum and manganese.  The maximum filter hydraulic capacity is 21 gpm.  After filtration, the water is chlorinated with sodium hypochlorite, delivered to the storage tank, and gravity fed to the system.  A radio telemetry system controls water storage tank liquid level.  The infiltration gallery is periodically (weekly) backwashed to remove silt and debris.  When backwashing can no longer effectively remove the silt, the drain rock in the gallery is replaced (about once every 10 years).

This system serves the Warner Valley Ranger Station.  It consists of a surface water influenced spring source, two 1500-gallon polypropylene water tanks, a bag filtration system including a roughing filter, a prefilter, and a Giardia filter, and a solar-powered hypochlorinator.  The system operates entirely by gravity.  Water flows from the existing spring to the treatment building where it is filtered (3 gpm) and disinfected.  The treated water flows into the water tanks for storage and chlorine contact time and then into the distribution pipe to the Ranger Station.

The system consists of a drilled well (drilled in 2020), two in-line water filters, a hypochlorinator for chlorine disinfection, 2 filters for sediment, 2 pressure tanks, and distribution piping consisting of a mixture of black PE, PVC, and galvanized iron most of which is believed to be 1¬º‚Äù in diameter.

This year-round system serves a residence and several yard hydrants and livestock water troughs.  It consists of a drilled well, sodium hypochlorite disinfection equipment, a large bladder-type hydropneumatic tank, and 3-inch pvc distribution piping.  When the system pressure reaches pump-on, a pressure switch energizes the well pump.  Water is pumped from the well through an enclosure containing the disinfection equipment which injects sodium hypochlorite.  The treated water enters the distribution piping.  When the pressure reaches pump-off, the pressure switch de-energizes the well pump.  Contact time is provided within the piping before the first point of use.  Power is provided by a combination propane-powered generator/photovoltaic system.

Improvements are planned for the water system.  The water facilities serve the residence.  The system consists of a 6-inch diameter, 100-foot deep drilled well with a submersible pump, disinfection equipment, hydropneumatic tank, two 4,000-gallon galvanized steel water storage tanks, and 2-inch pvc water line from the tanks to the residence.  The well, disinfection equipment, and hydropneumatic tank are located in a lockable fiberglass enclosure.  The submersible pump delivers water at 20 gpm from the well to the storage tanks via a dedicated fill line.  Sodium hypochlorite solution is injected into the water before discharging into the tank.  A propane-powered generator operates the well pump to fill the water storage tanks.  Water then flows by gravity to the residence.

This year-round system is operated by the California State University Desert Studies Center (DSC) under a contract with the park.  The park has entered into a cooperative agreement with DSC regarding operation of the water system.  DSC is responsible for the day-to-day operation of the system, including all required water quality monitoring.  The park is responsible for any major system facility improvements.  

There are two separate water systems.  One system provides potable water to hose bibbs, toilet and shower facilities in two residences and two dormitories, and communal kitchen.  The other system delivers untreated well water to maintain the water level in the fish pond.  A common drilled well serves as the source for both systems.  Two submersible pumps are installed in the well, one for each system.

The potable water system consists a submersible pump, three 2,500-gallon polyethylene water storage tanks, water treatment facilities consisting of a water softener, a 1-micron cartridge filter, reverse osmosis membrane filtration (RO), chlorination equipment, and distribution piping.  The untreated water fills the water storage tanks via a dedicated 3-inch PVC fill line.  The water tanks are plumbed to allow any one tank to be removed for maintainance without disruption of service.  Two separate lines feed the potable connections in the distribution system.  One line serves the kitchen and the other feeds the remaining potable connections.  Each has its own chlorinator to inject sodium hypochlorite.  An RO membrane filters the water feeding the kitchen, since the well water is highly mineralized and unpalatable.  Water filtered by the RO filter is stored in a separate 300-gallon polyethylene.  On demand, an in-line flow switch energizes the chlorinator which injects sodium hypochlorite for disinfection.  The filtered and chlorinated water flows by gravity to a faucet in the kitchen.  There is no commercial grid power available at Zzyzx, so power is provided by a combination of a wind charger, a solar array, and several generators.  The RO membrane is removed once per year and sent to manufacturer for inspection and maintenance.  The RO unit is also disinfected at this time.

This system serves a comfort station, drinking fountain,.  It consists of a groundwater well, disinfection equipment, two 120-gallon buried chlorine contact chambers, water distribution piping, and a 20,000-gallon above ground welded steel water storage tank.  A photovoltaic system with emergency propane backup generator provides electric power to all facilities.  Water is pumped by the well pump through a vault housing the disinfection equipment where sodium hypochlorite solution is injected.  The disinfected water then passes through the contact chambers before entering the distribution system piping.  There is no dedicated fill line to the water tank.  The water tank provides storage only, not volume for chlorine contact.

description: This year-round system serves the park facilities at Bear Gulch and Chalone Creek.  It consists of a drilled well with submersible pump, sodium hypochlorite disinfection system, a 20,000-gallon above-ground welded steel water storage tank serving the Chalone area, and a 60,000-gallon above-ground welded steel water storage tank serving Bear Gulch facilities. A float valve at the Chalone water tank controls flow into the tank.  A pressure reducer located in a separate building in the Chalone residential and maintenance area decreases the pressure between the Bear Gulch system and the Chalone water tank.

When called the well pump is energized and pumps water from the wells to the treatment building where a flow switch energizes the hypochlorinator to inject sodium hypochloride. Water is pumped at a rate of about 13 gpm from the well through the treatment building where sodium hypochlorite solution is injection and discharges into the water storage tank. This system provides water to both Glen Camp and Wildcat Camp. Water is pumped from the well through the upflow filter into the storage tank via a dedicated fill line.  The tank provides storage and chlorine contact time.  Liquid sodium hypochlorite is injected in the line near the wellhead.  Treated water then gravity flows to each campground via distribution piping. description: The water system serves a single family residence. The first booster pump delivers water from the wooden spring box to the large water storage tank.  The untreated water flows by gravity to the treatment building where a booster pump pumps it through the two filters.  The flow switch energizes the hypochlorinator which injects sodium hypochlorite solution before discharging into the smaller tank.  The small tank provide volume for contact time.  A second booster pump then pressurizes the water for use in the distribution piping.

The treatment room contains a 1-micron absolute micron cartridge filter (GE Osmonics SXE-10-EHS), hypochlorinator, booster pump and pressure tank. It then flows to the treatment room where the booster pump pumps it through the filter and the water is chlorinated with sodium hypochlorite solution. description: This system serves the headquarters and maintenance complexes and to the Visitor Information Center Overlook.  It consists of a raw-water intake from Whiskeytown Lake, a treatment building containing two multimedia pressure-filters, and post-chlorination equipment, a 60,000-gallon welded steel above ground water storage tank, and distribution system piping.  A 15 horsepower submersible pump at the lake intake pumps water to the treatment building where polymer is added to aid in filtration.  It then passes through the filters to remove turbidity.  The filtered water is chlorinated and then flows to the water tank via a dedicated 4-inch ductile iron fill line.  The water tank provides storage and chlorine contact time.  Treated water flows by gravity from the tank to the facilities.  The system is operated manually with a time clock set as necessary to keep the tank full.  Filter backwash water is used to irrigate the lawn around the headquarters building.  The surface water source turbidity for raw is grab-sampled and treated water is continually monitored.  Chlorine residuals of the treated water immediately after filtration are also continually monitored.    The distribution system consists of 4-inch ductile iron pipe and 6-inch PVC pipe. In 2020, a mixer was added to the water storage tank.

description: The water system serves a drinking fountain in the HSC, flush toilets, showers, employee laundry, the kitchen facilities, and a drinking fountain and two flush toilets in the backpackers campground.  It consists of a surface water intake in the Merced River, treatment building with chlorine disinfection equipment and a sand filtration system, a 2.5-gpm slow sand filter, a 1,500-gallon polyethylene surge tank, a 1,500-gallon polyethylene contact tank, a 1,550-gallon polyethylene storage tank, and distribution piping.  Raw water flows by gravity from the intake to the treatment facility.  An air relief valve at the high point in the line bleeds air to prevent air lock.  Before entering the building a separate line directs some of the raw water to the six flush toilets.  Another connection directs raw water to the hydrant by the septic tank for wash down.  The remaining raw water passes through the sand filter and into the surge tank.  When the water in the storage tank reaches low level and the surge tank low level float for booster shut off is above low water level, the booster pump pumps water from the surge tank through a 10-micron cartridge pre-filter and a 1-micron Giardia filter, is chlorinated and discharges to the chlorine contact tank then to the storage tank.  Flow through the bag filters is typically 14 gpm with new bag filters.  Water is then gravity fed to the distribution system.  All pumps and controls are powered by a photovoltaic system.  The water intake structure is built at the end of a channel off the river.  During normal river flows, water flow over the intake structure continually brings in fresh water.  During periods of low flow or drought, water does not flow through this channel.  A 100-foot extension must be connected to the intake to obtain water that is not stagnant.

This seasonal system serves the Tuolumne Lodge, store, NPS campground, visitor center, NPS staff housing, and concessions housing.  It consists of a dam water impoundment on a creek, a sedimentation/flocculation/screen basin, chemical addition for flocculation, two multimedia pressure filters, hypochlorinator for disinfection, a 100,000-gallon welded steel above ground water storage tank, and a 10,000-gallon bolted galvanized steel backwash holding tank.  When called by a float switch in the water tank, water flows by gravity from the source intake structure into the sedimentation basin where polyphosphate is injected for flocculation.  The floc settles in the basin.  The water then flows through three screens of increasingly finer mesh to the water treatment building where a pump increases pressure to enhance flow through the two pressure filters.  The filtered water is then injected with sodium hypochlorite solution and discharges into the water tank via a dedicated fill line for contact time and storage.  The filtered and disinfected water is then fed by gravity to the facilities.  A backwash pump forces treated water from the water tank back through the filters, discharging into the backwash tank where sediments settle.  Backwash water is then discharged to the sanitary sewer.

A separate water system provides water to NPS staff housing during the winter.  It consists of a drilled well, 3 filters (50 micron, 1 micron, carbon), a pressure tank, and distribution system.

The Ostrander Hut is a backcountry facility used during the winter season.  It provides shelter for approximately 40 visitors and a resident host.  Water for the host residence is drawn from the lake by a submersible pump and delivered to the hut water through a 2-inch PE pipe.  The raw lake water then passes through a 50 micron filter and ¬Ω micron filter before being stored in an 80-gallon galvanized steel water tank located on the second floor of the hut.  The pump is connected to the intake line and operated manually to fill the water storage tank.  The pump is removed when the tank is full.  Water flows by gravity to the sink in the host‚Äôs kitchen.  The water is not disinfected.  Visitors obtain drinking water by melting snow.  They are instructed to boil and/or filter it before using for potable purposes.

This seasonal public non-community serves three comfort stations at the Bridalveil Creek Campground.  It consists of a drilled well, treatment building with disinfection equipment, a buried steel water storage tank, and distribution system piping.  A submersible pump pumps water from the well to the treatment building where a hypochlorinator injects sodium hypochlorite solution into it. description: This seasonal system serves the concession store, snack bar and restrooms, visitor comfort station, and seasonal employee residential area.  It consists of two surface water sources, a treatment building containing a pressure sand filter, bag filtration, and hypochlorinator, a 300,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank, a 10,000-gallon bolted steel water storage tank, and distribution system piping.  At the beginning of the season, water from the Pothole Meadow surface water intake flows by gravity to the treatment building where polymer is injected before flowing through a pressure sand filter.  The filtered water is then disinfected using sodium hypochlorite solution and flows into the large water tank for storage and contact time.  The treated water then feeds the distribution system by gravity.  The sand filter is backwashed manually as needed.  The backwash water is discharged down the slope to daylight.  As conditions dry and the Pothole Meadow source is unable to meet demand, the source at Union Point is used.  Water behind an impoundment dam flows by gravity via a 4-inch pvc line to a holding tank at Union point.  A 10 hp positive displacement pump lifts water via a 4-inch galvanized line to the 10,000-gallon tank by the treatment building.  A booster pump in the treatment building then pumps the water through the treatment building where it is filtered and disinfected before being discharged into the large water tank.  The system has no automatic controls.   A valve is throttled to control flow.  When the tank is full and flow in exceeds demand treated water flows out the tank overflow and discharges to daylight.

description:
This system serves a variety NPS structures, including 19 housing units, visitor center, campground, maintenance area, and ranger building/fire cache structure.  Water is supplied by the Cave Springs Well (WS004), which produces approximately 26 gallons per minute.  The well is 78 feet deep with a static water level of 11 feet (1990).  The well casing is 6" diameter PVC and is screened from 35 feet to the bottom of the well with 6" diameter PVC screen.

The sourcewater has the following water quality issues: 
-	Total dissolved solids (TDS) = 505 mg/L (Date of test: 1990). > Secondary maximum contaminant level (MCL) of 500 mg/L
-	Total dissolved solids (TDS) = 1170 mg/L (Date of test: 2002). > Secondary MCL of 500 mg/L
-	Hardness = 235 mg/L (Date of test: 1990). Very hard water.
-	Iron = 0.38 mg/L (Date of test: 1990). > Secondary MCL of 0.3 mg/L

From the well, the water is pumped to the water treatment building where potassium permanganate is injected for oxidation of the iron and two multi-media filters (Carbon, Multi-Media, and Greensand) are used to remove the iron.  The water is then chlorinated and stored in three fiberglass 20,000 gallon underground storage tanks located behind the treatment building.  The water is then pressurized using three 3 HP booster pumps and five WX -350 pressure tanks (119 gallons each) for distribution to the park.  Two 10 HP fire pumps are used for high flows.  A separate booster pump in the pumphouse is used to provide pressure to two 119 gallon pressure tanks at each campground comfort station (comfort station A & B) through a pressure sustaining valve and is controlled by pressure switches located in the pumphouse.  Backwash water from the filters is discharged into a lined evaporation pond.  The backwash water is pumped through a soaker hose located about mid-depth on the lagoon liner to promote evaporation of the backwash water.

description:
There is one water system that serves all of Mesa Verde National Park.  The source water is Mancos Creek, a mountain stream located above Mancos, CO.  A water intake was constructed above Jackson Lake in 2003 and modified in 2008.  The park is currently drawing all of its water from this location.  

The intake is made up of infiltration beds consisting of two banks of infiltrators beneath the river, diversion walls to slow water flow across the beds, sedimentation basin, and associated valving.  The system is designed to allow the operator to adjust the level of water over the beds.  This site is very remote with no unauthorized vehicular access, although the area is frequented by hikers and fisherman.  The park also has the capability of drawing from an alternate intake (Jackson Lake) if needed.

From the intake, the raw water gravity flows through a raw water transmission pipe a distance of about 17 miles to the surface water treatment plant located at the entrance to the park.  Water is stored in two 25,000 gallon raw water storage tanks near the entrance gate before flowing by gravity to the water treatment plant.  

The park installed a Pall Aria microfiltration system in the spring of 2006 capable of producing 150 gpm.  The new plant is automated to all aspects of the process, records the data for reporting requirements, and shuts the plant off if any parameters are exceeded.  The cleaning of the system is also fully automated when a preset quantity of water is processed or a preset pressure drop occurs across the membranes.  The backwash water is stored in two concrete basins before being discharged behind the plant; a NPDES permit is in place for the discharge.  Two 9,000 pound GAC filters were added in 2010 to remove organics that contribute to formation of disinfection byproducts.  The water is chlorinated using gas chlorination before distribution.

After treatment, three 60 HP high pressure (over 600 psi) booster pumps then pump the water to the top of the mesa to the 2 million gallon water storage tank (aka Navajo Hill Tank) near Far View.  From the Navajo Hill Water Tank, water flows by gravity to 3 water storage tanks (300,000 gallon storage tanks at Morefield, 300,000 gallon tank at Wetherill, and a 100,000 gallon tank at Chapin Mesa).  Water is hauled from the water system to a 2,700 gallon HDPE water storage tank at Cliff Palace where it is pressurized using solar powered booster pumps and a pressure tank to serve 2 drinking water fountains.

description: The Headquarters West system services a housing area, maintenance area, corral, and Kawuneechee Visitor Center. In the treatment building water flows through a check valve and has lime injected and then flows into a mixing tank with an air relief valve. It then has liquid sodium hypochlorite added as it progresses to a second mixing tank with an air relief valve. The water then progresses to an ion exchange tank with MTM (manganese dioxide filtering media) and garnet media. The line then splits with one line running to Tank A and the other to Tank B. The line proceeding to Tank A flows through a meter then to a 50,000 gallon tank. Tank A services the campground and the Moraine Park Livery. The Tank A portion of the system is a seasonal operation. The line heading to Tank B, branches off and feeds three residences and a museum building. The line continues onto Tank B which is a 10,000 gallon in ground concrete tank. Tank B then flows to the High Drive area which services 7 residences and fills a 3,000 gallon water storage tank from the bottom. Tank B also flows to a 100,000 and 150,000 gallon underground concrete tanks that are operated in series but can be isolated. These tanks service the headquarters, housing, maintenance, and livery operations in the headquarters area.

description: The water system at Aspenglen campground services a campground (4 comfort stations, 50 campsites without hookups, and 2 seasonal residences) and the Smith Sisters area (2 seasonal residences).
