water_system_name: 335266 Water System Fall River Pass - AVC
description: The Alpine Visitor Center and Trail Ridge Store are currently serviced by a groundwater source. The 600 foot well (8 GPM) is located near the power building. The water is pumped to the treatment area in the power building and the water flows through a meter and has liquid sodium hypochlorite injected and then flows to the 60,000 gallon tank. From the 60,000 gallon concrete in ground tank water is pumped to both the distribution system and a 20,000 gallon concrete in ground storage reservoir that floats on the system.

The water system at Glacier Basin Campground services a 149 site and 14 group site campground without hookups, and a couple of host sites with hookups, an RV dump station, 11 comfort stations, hose bibs throughout the campground, a ranger station, two seasonal residences, the livery and bunkhouses at Glacier Creek, and a picnic area and comfort station at Sprague Lake.

Water is obtained through a drilled well and passes through a filter housing (used to contain a strainrite bag filter (HPM99-CC-2SR)) to a UV system (Sanitron Model #S2400B) to a meter and a check valve and has liquid sodium hypochlorite injected into the water.  The water line then splits with one lateral running to the Glacier Basin Campground, where the water flows through an automatic valve, a check valve, a meter, and then to a 57,000 gallon glass lined bolted steel water tank that then flows back to the distribution system.

The other lateral first flows past the livery to Sprague Lake.  The water passes through an automatic valve and a meter at the treatment building then progresses downstream.  At the livery the water is teed off of the main line and flows through a 50 micron cartridge filter to a variable feed drive pump to two Air-E-Tainer (Model 566) hydropneumatic tanks and then splits to the men's bunkhouse and through a pressure reducing valve to the women's bunkhouse.

The line continues further downstream to Sprague lake.  As the water enters the Sprague Lake area it flows through a check valve, a meter, and then to a 5,000 gallon above ground fiberglass tank that floats on the system.

The Green Pipeline system services six seasonal NPS residences and seven inholding residences. description: The Park Headquarters Water System, also known as the Everglades Shores Water System and Ochopee Water System, consists of two wells, 75 gallon hydropneumatic tank, polyphosphate injection, 1-mile transmission main, chlorine injection system, gravity tower aeration, two 6,000 gallon above ground water storage tanks, three distribution pumps, and distribution system. In the event that rainwater is not available, water is pumped from Biscayne Bay, treated through the RO system, and enters the storage tanks. This system is a non-potable system and does not include chlorination.  This system serves the Boca Chita Key Comfort Station, which only has toilets and no sinks. description: The Fort Jefferson Water System provides both potable and non-potable water to Fort Jefferson on Garden Key.  The potable water system consists of a 2-inch PVC ocean intake, dual 1.5 hp pressure pumps, cartridge filters, reverse osmosis (RO) system, buried 37,000 gallon storage tank, four 80-gallon hydropneumatic tanks (two prior to RO and two after storage), and a distribution system.  The ocean intake is located in the Fort's moat and protected by the sea wall. The raw water is pumped through a series of 20 and 5-micron cartridge filters, and two 80-gallon hydropneumatic tanks prior to arriving at the RO system.  The RO system is a package plant that includes 20 and 5-micron cartridge filters, a charcoal filter, and the RO membrane filters that have a flowrate of approximately 1.5 to 2.5 gallons per minute.  The RO brine waste is discharged to the original Fort Jefferson drainfield, which is not part of the Fort Jefferson Septic System.  The finish water is pumped to the buried storage tank where a floating tablet chlorinator is used for disinfection.  From the storage tank, water is pumped through two 80-gallon hydropneumatic tanks and into the distribution system.  The 37,000 gallon potable water storage tank makes up one compartment of a three compartment tank.

description: The Loggerhead Key Water System consists of an ocean intake, pumphouse with 60-gallon hydropneumatic tank, cartridge filters, reverse osmosis (RO) system, UV disinfection, chlorine injection system, two 500-gallon water storage tanks, and a distribution system.  In 2017, erosion damage and concerns led to the ocean intake being modified to use a flexible pipe on the beach and the intake pump being moved from the Boathouse to the new pumphouse.  The raw water is pumped through a 60-gallon hydropneumatic tank and 20 and 5-micron cartridge filters prior to arriving at the RO system.  The RO system is a package plant that includes UV disinfection and has a maximum flowrate of approximately 0.5 gallons per minute.  The finish water is pumped passes through the chlorine injection point and into the plastic storage tanks, which are located in the treatment buildings. The distribution system includes a 3/4 hp distribution pump and 60-gallon hydropneumatic tank.   This system serves the 1926 House and Kitchen House.

description: The Flamingo Water System consists of two 40-ft deep wells with dual 40 hp submersible pumps, a water treatment plant with chlorine disinfection, 550 gallon transfer tank, two 10,000 hydropneumatic tanks, a 248,000 gallon steel bolted water storage tank, and a distribution system.  The treatment plant is required as the groundwater is naturally saline. The treatment system is capable of producing finished water at 275 GPM and consists of cartridge filtration followed by reverse osmosis (RO) membrane filters, a degassifier (hydrogen sulfide removal), calcite system, and sodium hydroxide, sodium hypochlorite, and corrosion inhibitor injection systems.  On average the treatment plant processes between 20,000 and 30,000 gallons of finished water daily.  Approximately 35% of raw water becomes finished water, while the remainder is RO brine that is disposed of at the Flamingo Wastewater System.  A continuous chlorine analyzer monitors residuals in water sent to the storage tank and a SCADA system is used to monitor and operate treatment system components.  The treatment plant was built in 2005, the steel storage tank in 2004, and the RO units were replaced in 2013.  Several minor system components were replaced in 2017 after Hurricane Irma damaged the water system.  This system serves the Flamingo area, which includes the Flamingo Marina, store, employee housing, maintenance yard, Visitor Center, and campground.

description: The Fort Pickens Water System consists of two water wells, two ground level water storage tanks, chlorine disinfection, distribution system, and two automatic flushing hydrants.  The two wells extend to an estimated depth of 150 ft.  Well No. 1 was original to the system (year built is unknown), while Well No. 2 was built in 2007 as part of a larger rehabilitation project needed after the system was damaged in Hurricane Ivan in 2004.  The 2007 project also included a new water plant, water tank, replacement of some distribution lines, the removal of a gas chlorination system, and installation of a liquid hypochlorite chlorination system.  Water sampling has shown that Well No. 2 has elevated levels of naturally occurring ammonia.  Additionally, both wells have elevated levels of natural organic matter (NOM).  The two wells are used in rotation.  The chlorination system is located within the water treatment plant and includes two 100 gallon chlorine tanks and dosing pumps.  The two ground level water storage tanks are located next to the wells and have 8,000 and 10,000 gallon capacities.  After the storage tanks, the water is pumped into the 6-inch distribution main that ends at the Ranger Station near the park entrance.  The system serves the facilities in the vicinity of Fort Pickens on the Florida side of the Park.  The facilities served include staff housing, the Fort Pickens Visitor Center, three comfort stations, day use picnic areas, Mine Store, Ranger Station, and two campgrounds.

description:
The canyon area has several lodges, a variety of cabin rental units, a general store with grocery and restaurant, an Adventure Store, service station, visitor center, large campground, RV dump station, horse corral, and public laundry/ shower facility. Housing for NPS and concessionaire personnel is a variety of single family residences, dormitories, cabins, and a large trailer court. Most of these facilities are open on a seasonal basis. Winter activity includes a snowmobile warming hut and a winter camping concession.

Water is obtained from an intake structure on the Yellowstone River.  A raw water pump station is located in a vault at the river with three 30 HP pumps that pump water to a hypalon-lined open 1,000,000 gallon raw water settling reservoir located at the water treatment plant (WTP).  Water flows by gravity from the settling reservoir to the WTP, which was constructed in 1984-85.  The WTP is a conventional surface water filtration plant with coagulation/flocculation, sedimentation, and mixed-media filtration.  Soda ash is added for pH adjustment prior to coagulation/flocculation.  A polymer is also added at the beginning of the plant to aid in coagulation/flocculation and a filter aid is added prior to the filters to aid in filtration.  Liquid sodium hypochlorite is injected for disinfection.  A 24-inch diameter water main was installed after the WTP to achieve adequate chlorine contact time.  The filters are backwashed into one of two hypalon-lined backwash lagoons as needed.

The permit from EPA requires 95% of turbidity readings to less than 0.3 NTU, with 100% of turbidity readings less than 1.0 NTU.  The average daily water demand is approximately 230,000 gpd in the summer.  The WTP requires a level 2 water operator. Mammoth Hot Springs water system serves a full array of visitor services, many permanent and seasonal housing units, NPS and concession administrative offices, and a large maintenance area.  The system is classified as a public community surface water system.  An intake structure diverts surface water from Panther Creek and the Gardner River.  Water quality tends to be better from Panther Creek, so this is the primary water source.  Water is piped approximately 4 miles to the water treatment plant (WTP) and goes through a hydroelectric turbine before it enters an open raw water reservoir near the WTP.  

The WTP is a conventional filtration plant with coagulation/flocculation, sedimentation, and mixed media filtration with a design capacity of about 1 million gallons per day.  Potassium permanganate is added oxidize iron and manganese and a polymer is also added to improve filtration.  The filter media is backwashed as needed into 2 backwash ponds for evaporation. Sodium hypochlorite solution is injected for disinfection and enters a 34,000 gallon baffled treated water contact chamber/clearwell at the WTP for chlorine contact (CT) prior to distribution.  Storage is provided by a 160,000 gallon underground concrete storage tank (Upper Pressure Zone Tank) located at the WTP, which is connected to the clearwell.  A million gallon concrete underground storage tank with hypalon liner is located approximately 2 miles from the WTP, floats on the distribution system, and is filled after distribution system demand is met.

The permit from EPA requires 95% of turbidity readings to less than 0.3 NTU, with 100% of turbidity readings less than 1.0 NTU.  Water demand ranges from about 150,000 gpd in the winter to 450,000 gpd in the summer. The water treatment plant requires a level 3 water operator.  The park operates an EPA certified laboratory out of the Mammoth WTP that performs bacteriological testing for the entire park.

description:
The Old Faithful area is one of the major developed areas of the park.  A large array of visitor services are available.  There is also a housing area and a maintenance facility.  Potable water for Old Faithful is obtained from a raw water intake structure on the Firehole River.  Water flows by gravity to the water treatment plant (WTP).  The raw water quality varies dramatically and is difficult to treat consistently.  The raw water contains fluoride more than the secondary (aesthetic) standard of 2.0 mg/l but below the primary (health) standard or MCL of 4.0 mg/l.  A lined open 750,000 gallon sedimentation basin was constructed in 2007 that can be used during spring runoff when turbidity in the river is high. The system is a public community surface water system.  

The WTP is a conventional surface water treatment system with coagulation/flocculation, sedimentation, and mixed media filtration.  A polymer is added before filtration to improve the filtration process.  Ferric chlorine is added prior to filtration to help remove arsenic, but this increases the pH.  The treated water tends to be corrosive (pH about 6.0), so sodium hydroxide is added to the clearwell to increase the pH and help address elevated lead and copper concentrations in the distribution system.  Treated water is disinfected with liquid sodium hypochlorite as it flows into a 40,000 gallon clearwell.  There is no dedicated fill line to the reservoir but calculations show that CT requirements are being met largely because of the large WTP clearwell.  Filters are backwashed into 2 percolation/evaporation basins as needed.

The permit from EPA requires 95% of turbidity readings to less than 0.3 NTU, with 100% of turbidity readings less than 1.0 NTU.  The average daily water demand is approximately 250,000 gpd in the summer and 50,000 gpd during the winter.  The WTP requires a level 3 water operator.  The WTP has a capacity of about 450 gpm, or 324,000 gpd when operating 12 hours/day.  Water from the WTP is pumped to a 1.6 million gallon buried concrete reservoir that floats on the distribution system.

Lake Springfield is the surface water source of our drinking water.  It contains 17.6 billion gallons when full and covers about 4,200 acres. Its 265-square-mile watershed, including the Sugar and Lick Creek drainage areas, is composed primarily of agricultural land.  During times of low precipitation, water is pumped from the South Fork of the Sangamon River at its confluence with Horse Creek. A source water assessment for our supply has been completed by the IEPA. Information provided by this assessment indicates the vulnerability of our water supply to potential sources of contamination.  Causes of pollution to the lake include nutrients, siltation, suspended solids, and organic enrichment. Primary sources of pollution include agricultural runoff, land disposal (septic systems), and shoreline erosion. If you would like a copy of the assessment, call the Water Purification Plant at (217) 757-8630.

To convert this raw water supply to drinking water, lake water is pumped through CWLP‚Äôs Water Treatment Plant where chemical reactions are initiated to assist in the removal of algae, suspended solids, hardness and many chemical constituents. The clarification basins remove the bulk of these materials and the final filter beds remove very small particles. Fluoride is added to prevent tooth decay; chlorine to disinfect the finished water; and ammonia to stabilize the chlorine in the distribution system.

The usable storage of this tank is thought to be about 670,000 gallons.  This tank was constructed in 1978.  The Fox Ridge Tank is also a 2 million gallon standpipe with 670,000 of usable storage. description:
The Operations Section at the Topeka Water Treatment Facility uses various chemical and mechanical processes to transform raw water from the Kansas River into clean and safe drinking water. The first of these treatment processes is the elevation of raw river water into the treatment basins using water intake structures. The Topeka Water Treatment Facility has two intake structures that contain six pumps each. All water intake pumps have rated daily capacities of five to ten million gallons. A durable and heavyweight, small mesh traveling screen is positioned immediate the intake pumps to prevent entry of debris that may either damage mechanical equipment or impair chemical treatment processes.

The newest plant, the East-South Plant (1999), was constructed in parallel and identical design as the East-North Plant (1981). Many infrastructure improvements were added in 1999 to 2001. At the Topeka Water Treatment Facility, there are many shapes and sizes of basins and each is designed to provide controlled contact and settling time for each specific chemical or mechanical process. Depending on their location in the treatment scheme, individual basin capacities range from thousands of gallons to nearly three million gallons. The basins in each of the three treatment plants at the Topeka Water Treatment Facility are connected in series, with each adjoining basin slightly lower in elevation than the previous. This allows the water to continuously flow by gravity from the beginning of the treatment process to the end. The average detention time for an entire process cycle though each of the three treatment plants is nearly 24 hours. The first chemical used in the water treatment process at the Topeka Water Treatment Facility is a positively charged synthetic polymer. It is flash-mixed into the raw river water before it flows into the first sedimentation basin. The polymer effectively attracts and enmeshes negatively charged turbidity particles in raw river water and causes them to settle. A large blow-down located at the center of the polymer sedimentation basin is activated at timed intervals to dispel settled and collected solids. This process reduces the amount of suspended material or turbidity significantly.

The partially processed water then flows by gravity to the disinfection contact basin. Chlorine is added at the disinfection contact basin to destroy any bacteria or viruses that may be present. Ammonia is subsequently added at a specified entry point after chlorine addition to form the secondary distribution disinfectant, chloramine. A series of baffles in the disinfection contact basin provide effective contact and reaction time to ensure that the destruction of pathogens is complete. The controlled application of chlorine and ammonia in the absence of sunlight reduces the level of disinfection by-products below regulatory requirements. These small, covered and baffled treatment units are also designed to be economically and easily retrofit as regulations progress and alternative disinfectants such as chlorine dioxide and ozone are required.

The disinfected water then flows into the coagulation, flocculation and softening basins where lime and alum are added. Lime reacts with various dissolved minerals to form primarily two insoluble precipitates: calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide. Additionally, the softening process enmeshes, coagulates and settles smaller remaining particles and dissolved organic substances.

Alum is added to further aid and enhance coagulation. In the two east treatment plants, previously reacted solids in specialized solid contact basins provide improved softening precipitation and efficiency of chemical application.

Clarification basins have similar collection weirs, sweeps and blow-downs. The water is then diverted to large primary clarification basins that allow additional detention time for gravity to settle out remaining precipitates and suspended materials. Large sweeps slowly rotate along the entire bottom of these basins to collect and move settled precipitates and turbidity to a central collection area. Large blow-downs located at the center of the primary clarification basins are activated at timed intervals to dispel settled and collected solids.
After the primary clarification basin, carbon dioxide is bubbled in to stabilize and lower the pH of softened water. Controlled application of soda ash and phosphate is also added at the primary recarbonation basin to increase the alkalinity level and provide corrosion control. The water then flows into a second large clarification basin. This allows additional detention time for remaining suspensions and precipitates to settle. Center sweeps and blow-downs collect and remove additional settled solids.

After water exits the secondary clarifying basin, fluoride is added to supplement levels that occur naturally. Large rectangular filtration beds are located in the enclosed area behind the doors. Cleansing of the water through specialized filtration units completes the treatment process at the Topeka Water Treatment Facility. The small amounts of suspended fine particles that remain after secondary clarification are nearly all removed by processing the water through automated filtration units. The Topeka Water Treatment Facility has nearly 10,000 square feet of mixed layer filtration units containing approximately four feet of filtrating materials. Regular cleaning of the filter beds is accomplished by repeatedly forcing clean water up through filtration beds. Processed filtered water is stored in clearwell reservoirs located beneath the filters. To ensure the filtration process is optimized, turbidity meters continuously monitor finished water quality.

The suction shafts on these pumps are as long as twenty-seven feet. The Topeka Water Treatment Facility has nearly nine million gallons of underground reservoir storage and seven high service pumps with rated capacities from five to fifteen million gallons a day. These pumps transfer water from underground clearwells into four large transmission lines. These large arterial water lines branch out into a network of more than 800 miles of water mains that transport clean and safe drinking water every day.

description: The Visitor Center water supply is from a well that was drilled in 2010 with a total depth of 360 feet.The well pump is activated by a pressure tank switch. There is a chemical feed system for disinfection with sodium hypochlorite and a 120 gallon contact tank. The staff kitchen skin has a reverse osmosis unit and sediment filter. The upstairs is a living quarters unit with 2 bedrooms, a bathroom, and kitchenette. The water at this location has had an exceedance of uranium above the EPA SDWA maximun contaminant limit (MCL) of 30Œºg/L and radon above the 4,000 pCi/L (note: generally, radon is more of an inhalation concern than ingestion concern). Past water sample results can be located on the ACAD 2018 report conducted by the Office of Public Health. description: The Ranger III water system consists of a water storage tank, pressure tank, and booster pumps.  The water is taken at the park HQ in Houghton, MI.  The water there comes from the CITY OF HOUGHTON water system.  The City did not have any violations in 2012.

The microfiltration water system replaced the older Katydyn ceramic filter system.  The old system took water directly from Lake Superior through 10 micron bag filters that were periodically back-washed during the treatment process and then through a set of ceramic filters coated with diatomaceous earth.  This older system had extensive maintenance demands and struggled at times with the new EPA/State of Michigan surface water treatment rules.  The current microfiltration plant utilizes a barrier design consisting of 0.2 micron filter modules.  The system automatically backwashes itself and the maintenance demands are minimal.  The microfiltration system filtered water requires post chlorination only and that water is pumped to a chlorine contact tank near the pump house.  From there the water is pumped to a standpipe and again pumped to a elevated storage reservoir.  Potable water is distributed by gravity to the NPS headquarters area that consists of housing, apartments, dorms, administrative offices, recreational facilities and maintenance facilities.  

The operator of the treatment process is certified by the state and does an excellent job of ensuring the provision of safe drinking water to the staff located at Mott Island.  Treated water turbidity is 0.03 NTU or less.

description:
The water system at Rock Harbor has a conventional water treatment plant to treat water directly from Lake Superior.  The treatment process includes pre-chlorination and a chemical addition of alum that is rapid mixed to disperse the alum.  The water is allowed to flocculate.  The water is then filtered; post chlorinated and pumped to two ground-level bolted steel reservoirs.  A booster pump delivers the water to a new bolted steel standpipe located on a high ridge above the water treatment plant.  The water is then distributed by gravity to the following concession operations: 10 duplex housekeeping units, 58 lodge units located in four buildings, dormitory, dining room and snack bar, store, guest house, marina, public laundry, restrooms and showers.  Also water service is provided to the following NPS facilities: district ranger house, ranger office, seasonal employee house, maintenance office/break area, campground and utility service area.
  
Fire protection for the area is provided in a separate system that utilizes Lake Superior water.  There is no connection between the potable water system and the fire protection system.

The water treatment plant is located in the utility service area.  The water treatment plant houses a certified water test lab.  The lab performs routine water tests for the plant including bacteriological analysis.  This lab conducts all the water quality testing for the park's public and non-public water systems.  

The water treatment plant is well operated producing water with a turbidity of 0.1 NTU.  The chlorine levels are checked daily, the chlorine concentration is adequate to achieve proper CT values and all required reports are being sent to the state.  The laboratory certification from Michigan expires in 2012.

This is a non-public water system serving a ranger contact station.  The water is treated as non-potable.  The facility has public restrooms and there are no drinking fountains.  A bottled water cooler is provided and the restroom sinks are posted as non-potable water.

Source:
The source is a well of unknown construction.  The well has significant problems with silt and sand.

Treatment & Distribution:
There is no disinfection on this system.  After being pumped from the well there is a foot valve inside the basement of the building which is followed by a filter and sand trap, 2 pressure tanks, a 150 gallon storage tank.  The line supplying water to the building restrooms has an additional filter on in.  A separate line supplies water for sprinkler irrigation and has an RPZ installed on it to separate it from the rest of the system.

Source:  
The source is a spring (Tillet Spring) classified as groundwater.  The spring is located at the Tillet Fish Rearing Station which is operated by the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.   Water is collected in a concrete spring box and then piped ~1.7 miles under a state highway to a chlorination treatment building that is located within the park. The collection transmission main is 6 inch ductile iron that has been slip lined.   The spring water collection area is fenced and has a surface water diversion ditch.  Historic data and observation at Tillet Spring shows very little fluctuation of pH and water turbidity, indicating that the source is likely very stable and of high quality.  The collection structure is a 3‚Äôx3‚Äôx8‚Äô deep concrete vault with a gravel base.  Water collects in the vault and gravity flows to the chlorination building and on to the storage tank via a 4‚Äù poly main that was installed in 1996.  Two MPA tests were completed in the spring and fall of 2014 to assess the potential for surface water influence.  The MPA test results indicated a low risk for surface water influence and groundwater status was maintained.  In subsequent   communications from EPA it was made clear that EPA will continue to closely assess this source for potential surface water influence in the future and indicated that further MPA tests may be required based on survey assessments.  Proactive maintenance activities in order to maintain desirable vegetation, remove deep rooted woody vegetation, maintain fencing, maintain surface water diversion ditching and maintain the sanitary seal on the collection box hatch will be critical in order to maintain groundwater designation.

Treatment: 
 Water is chlorinated by chlorination injection pump system that is controlled by telemetric controls and a float switch in the reservoir.  After chlorination, water is delivered to the storage reservoir via gravity flow in a dedicated 4 inch poly line.  Chlorination can be by-passed in this system through use of a valve located outside the treatment building.  This by-pass system is used in the winter season to provide non-chlorinated water to the comfort stations for use by winter fishermen.  The winter-time water is labeled as NON-POTABLE in the comfort station.

Storage and Distribution:  
Treated water is stored in a 100,000 gallon above-ground steel reservoir.  Water is distributed to a campground with two loops and two comfort stations, the marina, playground and swimming beach.  The campground has to two host RV sites with full service hook-ups and has recently had 10 full service RV sites in each loop.

water_system_name: HBD Belly River Utilities Water System
description:
This water system is a remotely located backcountry non-public system using surface water.  It is approximately a 5 mile hike from the trailhead to the ranger station.  The system is serviced by a monthly trip from a maintenance operator. 

SOURCE:  
The water source is a small stream with a concrete intake structure constructed in the stream approximately 1000 feet east of the ranger station.  The intake structure contains 3 four-inch PVC perforated collection pipes overlain with 2 feet of gravel and sand. 

TREATMENT:
Water flows by gravity from the collection intake to a treatment facility where it is filtered with 3 stage cartridge filtration.  A 50 micron large pore cartridge filter, followed by chlorine injection, and then a 2-stage cartridge filtration bank of nominal 1 and absolute 1 micron filters. 

STORAGE: 
Storage is in a 220 gallon galvanized steel pressure tank.

DISTRIBUTION:
This system serves a ranger station, ranger residence, trail cabins, and an outside hose bib.  As a non-public system, the water is not made available to the public.

water_system_name: HBD Goat Haunt Utilities Water System
description:
SOURCE:
A 39' groundwater well with six inch casing and submersible pump (11 gpm).  Static water level is 20 feet.  The drawdown of the well fluctuates significantly seasonally and is reported to be as low as 35 feet during the late season.  The well is located between the government housing area and the horse corral.  The well is slightly downgrade from the corrals and ~200-400 yards from the corrals.  The area is heavily vegetated and the well has a good history of negative bacterial testing results and nitrate testing.   

TREATMENT:
Chlorinated by liquid hypochlorination injection pump located in a small building right next to the wellhead.  A 1 ¬Ω" HDPE dedicated fill line from the well to the tank and new control lines were installed during the 2002 season.

STORAGE:  
Storage is a 10,000 gallon steel tank.     

DISTRIBUTION:
This system serves a ranger station/border patrol station, visitor center, and seasonal residences.  A 6" HDPE distribution line from the tank was installed in 2002.

water_system_name: HBD Logan Pass Utilities Water System
description: The water system serves a Visitor Center, office, drinking fountains, one frost free hydrant, and comfort station.  Drinking water obtained from a sand infiltration gallery located approximately 1/2 mile west of the Visitor Center in the bed of Oberlin Creek. Water is collected in a concrete collection box and flows by gravity ~200 yards to the treatment building.  The water is filtered by two sets of parallel cartridge filters of 50 and 1 micron filters. There is no electrical power available at the treatment building, so disinfection is accomplished by a Dosatron flow driven chlorine injection pump. Due to the lack of electricity, there is no opportunity for continuous monitoring equipment at the treatment building. Turbidity, pH, and chlorine residuals are all monitored with grab samples and hand held metering equipment. The treated water is stored in a 10,000 gallon welded steel water storage tank.
point_of_use: Visitor Center, office, drinking fountains, one frost free hydrant, and comfort station

description:
The water system serves the Many Glacier Hotel, concessionaire housing, and concessionaire horse corrals.  Drinking water is provided by two wells classified as groundwater.  Well #1 is located approximately 125‚Äô north of Swiftcurrent Lake and is 61 feet deep with 6-inch diameter casing and slotted well screen located 54 to 59 feet below grade. An emergency fire flow system can serve the area by pumping water directly from Swiftcurrent Lake.

description:
The water system serves the campground and picnic area, ranger residence, and a RV dump station.  Drinking water is provided by a remotely located spring in rough terrain east of the campground.  Historically, the source was classified as groundwater under the influence of surface water.  A major rehabilitation of the collection box and raw water transmission main was completed in 2013.  Following two MPA tests in 2014, the source was re-designated as ground water.  

The spring box is constructed of galvanized steel with two 4 inch PVC schedule 40 well screen laterals.  The laterals are bedded in pea gravel and sand.  The entire spring collection area is covered with an impervious liner buried 6 inches to 1 ft subsurface.  The annular space around the circular spring box is sealed with bentonite.  There is a 6 inch drain and overflow line and the 4 inch raw water collection main with valves inside the spring box.  The 4 inch collection main flows by gravity through rough terrain to the treatment building near the campground.  High points in the collection main are fitted with air relief valves and low points have ball valves to facilitate draining.  The water is treated with a 5 micron and 1 micron absolute cartridge filters followed by chlorination and distribution. Liquid chlorination is provided via a flow driven injection pump. Chlorine contact time is provided by a section of pipe 24 inches in diameter and 140 feet long located immediately after chlorination and prior to the first service tap.
point_of_use: campground and picnic area, ranger residence, and a RV dump station

water_system_name: WLD Granite Chalet Utilities Water System
description:
Source: 
A surface water system utilizing an infiltration gallery on a stream located approximately 300 yards north of the chalet.  Water is collected behind a small concrete retention structure via 4" slotted pipe buried in a gravel bed and covered by filter fabric.  Raw water is delivered approximately 150 yards to the water treatment station via gravity flow through a 2 inch HDPE line that was installed new in 2015.  There is a separate drain line for the collection basin that daylights a few yards downgrade from the basin.  

Treatment:
Treatment consists of a course sediment filter (5 micron nominal) followed by an absolute 1 micron filter.  Filters are located on a small riser of galvanized line and are not enclosed in a structure.  Water is treated in batches by attaching a food grade hose to a post-filtration hydrant and filling a 100 gallon tank and adding a premeasured volume of 12% sodium hypochlorite to reach 0.2-1.0 mg/l free chlorine.  There are two 100 gallon storage tanks on site allowing one tank to be accessed and used by the public while the other tank is being treated and allowed to reach the the required contact time prior to use.  A new 100 gallon batch is produced each day during the operational season.  The unused portion of the previous day's batch is discarded each day prior to treating the new batch.

Important treatment conditions required by the MT DEQ Permit are as follows:
-  Ensure that no chlorinated water from discarded batches reaches surface water.  Use a dechlorinating agent if necessary.
- Temperature, pH, turbidity, and free chlorine residual must be recorded daily and reported using the appropriate forms provided by MT DEQ.
- Treatment must achieve a minimum of 92 minutes of contact time.
- Chlorination treatment must be to a level that maintains a minimum of 0.2 mg/l of free chlorine AFTER the contact time has been reached.
- Locking control valves must be used and in a locked-out position on the tank that is not currently in use for supplying potable water to the public.
 - Pre-filtration and post-filtration sample taps must have the handles removed, locked-out or otherwise inaccessible  whenever NPS operators are not present in order to prevent the public from taking untreated water from these taps.
source_notes: Source of water is an infiltration gallery. For our purposes this is classified as shallow groundwater with the type being the original source, and the aquifer is the top formation for this area.

description:
The water system serves headquarters, NPS HQ Residential area, wastewater treatment facility, NPS & Concessions Horse Corrals, shops and housing, Apgar Village, Apgar Campground and the town of West Glacier.  Drinking water is provided by the Rubideau spring located approximately 2 miles west of Headquarters and is classified as groundwater. MPA analysis supports the groundwater designation. The water collection system at the spring was rehabilitated in 2004-2005. Water from the spring is collected by a buried infiltration gallery and covered collection box. During seasonally high groundwater in the spring area, surface water flows over the top of the spring box structure. The spring box is equipped with pressure relief valves in the top of the concrete structure.

Water from the spring flows by gravity under McDonald Creek to a chlorination house where it is chlorinated with liquid sodium hypochlorite and then flows by gravity to two 100,000 gallon buried concrete reservoirs. Water tank levels are controlled by valves with telemetry elevation controls.  The system also has a supplementary re-chlorination facility that is designed to monitor chlorine residuals in the storage tanks and supplement by pumping water in a closed loop between the re-chlorination facility and the reservoir tanks. The re-chlorination capacity has not been used for several years.  There is no dedicated post-treatment fill line to the water storage reservoirs. All service connections are prior to storage tanks.

description:
SOURCE: An infiltration gallery consisting of a shallow dug well located approximately 10 feet from the edge of Bowman Creek.  The source is classified as Ground Water Under the Direct Influence of Surface Water.   The infiltration well is is a 36 inch diameter Corrugated Metal Pipe (CMP) set inside a 48 inch diameter CMP.  The void between the CMPs is filled with cement grout.  Two lids protect the top of the source from direct access.  Water is collected through perforations in the lower section of the CMP.  

A submersible pump in the well is controlled by water level floats in the storage tank.  A new 15 gpm Franklin submersible pump was installed in 2015.  Due to problems with recharge rate in the well, a Franklin Pumptec solid state pump protection system was installed at the same time.

TREATMENT: Water is pumped from the infiltration gallery to a treatment room where it is chlorinated and filtered with 5 micron and absolute 1 micron filters. Treated water is pumped to a storage tank via a dedicated fill line.   

STORAGE: Storage is an unbaffled 10,000 gallon buried fiberglass tank. Water from storage tank is distributed to service connections by gravity flow. 

DISTRIBUTION: The system serves a Ranger Station, comfort station, drinking fountain, and several seasonal residences.  The park has a special status from the primacy agency that allows the water system to be public (Transient, Non-Community) in the summer and non-public in the winter.

description: The water system serves the Sperry Chalet and kitchen.  Drinking water is provided by an infiltration gallery in a spring/creek that is supplied by glacial melt about 300 yards south of the chalet. The dam and pond at the infiltration gallery is lined with a hypalon polypropylene liner and the intake perforated pipe is embedded in gravel/sand that is covered with filter fabric. An older spring/infiltration gallery is also still connected to the system. The older spring is also supplied by glacial melt and is used as back-up source if the primary spring does not produce sufficient volume. Water from the spring flows to the treatment facility by gravity flow and is treated with cartridge filters (5 micron and 1 micron absolute) followed by chlorination.  The treated water flows into an 18,000 gallon steel water storage tank located next to the treatment building.

description:
Source:  
The source for this year round public water system is a shallow well (constructed approximately 1979) supplied by a shallow infiltration gallery located in the flood plain and in close proximity to the Little Big Horn River.  The infiltration lines are buried in shallow alluvium adjacent the Bighorn River and composed of sand, gravel, and shale.  The well is 6‚Äô in diameter and approximately 26‚Äô deep and is located in a pump house next to the infiltration gallery.  Details regarding the collection laterals are sparse and historical reports indicate 4 laterals 150 ft. in length with burial depth around 17 ft.  A more recent lateral addition extends generally to the west in a T-shape consisting of over 540 ft. of 6 Inch bituminous coated perforated CMP piping.  Current operators believe that this newer T-shaped infiltration lateral is supplying the system water and that all old laterals have been physically disconnected from the well although this is unconfirmed.  Water is pumped from the well by two vertical turbine pumps.  The pumps are controlled by water level in the large storage tank.  
The source water is classified as groundwater not under the influence of surface water.  This classification is based on two Microscopic Particulate Analyses (MPA) completed in 1993.  The results of those MPA tests found a low-risk for surface water influence.  A 1995 letter from the Montana DEQ confirms the designation as groundwater.  Two additional MPA tests were completed in 2018 and both scored a 0-Low Risk for surface water influence.  The source water is high in iron and definite seasonal fluctuations in quality and quantity are noted by the operators.  During some years, the well pumps have to be shut down and operated manually in order to keep water in the well especially late in the summer/fall.

Treatment:  
Water is pre-chlorinated immediately with a 12.5% sodium hypochlorite solution for the purpose of iron oxidation and precipitation.  After chlorination, water is pumped via a 6" main uphill approximately ¬º mile to the administration area where it is passed through an iron removal filter system (parallel train of 16 Kinetico brand Macrolite 2000 filters) for removal of precipitated iron.  The filters are housed in the maintenance building.  The filters automatically backwash based on gallons treated and backwash water is collected in a manifold that discharges to an old on-site wastewater system.  
After the iron removal filters, water either enters a "non-potable" system serving fire suppression and irrigation needs or else enters the potable or domestic side of the water system.  Water entering the domestic side of the system can enter either directly from the 6" main or from a 100,000 gallon reservoir that stores excess chlorinated but non-potable water.  In either case, all water entering the domestic side of the system is re-chlorinated prior to entering the 10,0000 gallon domestic water storage tank.

Storage:  
Water on the non-potable fire suppression and irrigation side of the system is stored in a 100,000 gallon buried concrete storage tank located near the visitor center.   After re-chlorination, domestic water is stored in a 10,000 gallon buried fiberglass tank located in the administration area.   

Distribution:  
The domestic side of the system serves an administrative office building/residential area, maintenance area, visitor center, and comfort station.  The non-potable side serves fire suppression needs and irrigation needs both in the cemetery and the administrative area.   Underground sprinkler systems are used for irrigation both in the administrative/residential area as well as the cemetery.    
There are four different underground sprinkler connections in the administrative/residential area.  Three are connected to the non-potable side of the system and one is connected to the domestic side.  The cemetery irrigation system is served by a separate 500 gallon storage tank and pump system that is connected to the non-potable side of the system.

description: The Visitor Center Water System is a seasonal system operational between April and November, which consists of a single 460-ft deep well, air stripper to remove sulfur gas, chlorine injection system, 1,000 gallon holding tank, pressure pump, four 260 gallon hydropneumatic tanks, chlorine booster station, and distribution system.  Well production is logged and is generally between 4,000 and 6,000 gallons per month.  The chlorine disinfection system uses a dosing pump and liquid sodium hypochlorite.  The chlorine booster station, installed in 2016, uses calcium hypochlorite tablets and is located at the end of the distribution line near the volunteer housing.  The system serves the volunteer buildings, Keeper's Quarters, Visitor Center, and bathhouse.
point_of_use: Volunteer buildings, Keeper's Quarters, Visitor Center, and bathhouse
treatment_system_type: Air stripper to remove sulfur gas, Chlorination
source_notes: Well is located in the lower confined aquifer - medium - to coarse-grained limestone of Oligocene age. "The beds of clay, silty clay, and clayey sand that overlie and confine the lower confined aquifer correlate with the Pungo River Formation of early and middle Miocene age. (Winner, 1978)

description: The Fort Raleigh Water System consists of two wells, two chlorination systems, six 50 gallon hydropneumatic tanks, 100,000 gallon above ground concrete raw water storage tank, two booster pumps, 3,000 gallon hydropneumatic tank, and distribution system.  Additionally, after the storage tank, two fire pumps are installed to provide backup pressure in case fire flow is needed.  The primary chlorination system is located prior to the storage tank and the other is used as a chlorine booster system prior to the 3,000 gallon hydropneumatic tank.  The chlorine dosing tanks have a 35 gallon capacity.  The six 50 gallon hydropneumatic tanks are typically offline and only used as backup when the storage tank is taken offline. This system serves all facilities within the Fort Raleigh National Historic Site, which includes the Park's Headquarters, Visitor Center, maintenance area, five staff quarters, Visitor Center Comfort Station, two VIP RV pads, The Elizabethan Gardens, and Waterside Theatre, which has two comfort stations, three food concessions and various support buildings.

It was located indoors and had a vertical turbine pump installation (Peerless Pump, model 10MA-2STG, 400 gpm). Treatment consisted of iron removal and disinfection. The water system for Carlsbad Cavern is classified as a Public Non-Community, Non-Transient Water System (PWSID 3549408).  A single source provides water to two distinct components.  The Cave Component serves the Visitor Center, Cavern Supply Restaurant and Gift Shop, the Big Room snack bar and public restrooms, water treatment building, administrative offices, maintenance area, comfort station, and staff residential housing.  The much smaller Rattlesnake Springs Component is served with a lateral from the old pumphouse near the well head.

Water for both system components is pumped from a groundwater well located in the Rattlesnake Springs area to a 250,000-gallon water storage tank.       Water is treated with sodium hypochlorite at the well head.

The 250,000-gallon tank provides contact time prior to delivery to the distribution system. Water is pumped from the 250,000-gallon water storage tank by a booster station into the water distribution system. A 315,000-gallon glass-fused-to-steel water tank, which floats on the distribution system, provides storage for this component.  A water softener and polyphosPHSte injection system installed at the treatment building has been taken off line due to problems created in the distribution system.  

Water supplied to the facilities in the Cavern Big Room passes through two (2) pressure reducing valves in parallel in the Cavern pump room that reduces pressure from 430 psi to 80 psi.  The utility lines from the surface to the Caverns are located in conduits in a vertical shaft in front of the Visitor Center.  The spaces between the conduits are filled with grout.  A short tunnel connects the bottom of the shaft to the Cavern pump room. Connections to surface utilities are located in a below-grade vault at the top of the shaft.  The vault is designed to drain to the surface.  A portable pump is available to remove water in the event of a line break.  There is an alarm system installed to signal pump failure.  A float valve has been installed in a small tank at the base of the vertical shaft so that when water is detected, a signal will be sent to the solenoid valve to stop the flow.  This prevents undetected flooding in the event of a line break when no one is on duty.

There are 6 testable backflow devices in the park as follows:  VC double check valve for fire suppression system, VC RPZ for boiler, VC Cave wet well washdown RPZ, VC Cave wastewater pump packing RPZ, Booster Station double check valve for fire suppression system, and an RPZ for the irrigation system.

Water is pumped from a well in the residential area through a pumphouse where it is disinfected with a sodium hypochlorite solution. description:
The park water system provides water to all park facilities including Visitor Center, the residential area, RV dump station, the maintenance area, wilderness trail crew quarters, Lower Scorpion campground, Upper Scorpion campground, and drinking fountain at the visitor contact station at the Monument trailhead.

Water is pumped from a well at Woody‚Äôs Corral through a water treatment building where it is disinfected with a sodium dichloro-s-triazinetrione solution.  The well is 100 feet deep with a 6-inch diameter casing and perforations from 25 to 80 feet.  From the treatment building the water is pumped through a 200 gallon chlorine contact tank to a 55,000-gallon bolted glass-fused-to-steel tank, via a dedicated fill line (except for the water main serving the corrals, campgrounds, and contact station).  An older 50,000 gallon welded steel tank has been taken offline, but can be manually filled for fire-fighting purposes.  The 50,000 gallon tank is equipped with an air gap on the tank fill line for backflow protection and is physically disconnected from the distribution system.  System controls are provided by a radio telemetry system.  A pressure transducer in the 55,000 gallon tank senses water pressure from the tank and energizes the well pump at low pressure (low water level) and de-energizes the pump at high pressure (high water level).  Water is delivered from the water storage tank to the park facilities via a distribution system consisting of 6-inch DI pipe.  An older well, the Middle Fork well, is physically disconnected from the water system, appears to be in a floodplain, and is unavailable in its current condition.

description:
The Gran Quivira water system is a Public Non-Community Transient water system that provides water to the visitor center, adjacent comfort station, residential area, and 2 RV sites.  The system consists of a well, pumphouse, water storage tank, and water distribution system.  A submersible well pump pumps water through the pumphouse (constructed in 1999) where it is disinfected with sodium hypochlorite.  It then passes through a dedicated 2-inch PVC water line to fill a 50,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank.  The tank was renovated in 2020.  Water flows by gravity from the tank into the water distribution system, which consists of 6-inch asbestos cement (AC) pipe that is reduced to a 2-inch PVC pipe from the old visitor center to the new visitor center.  System controls consist of electrodes located in the water storage tank that are hard wired to a control panel located in the pumphouse.  Three electrodes control pump-on, pump-off, low water level alarm, and high water level alarm.

A below grade double-check valve assembly provides backflow protection for the visitor center interior fire suppression system.

description:

The system consists of a well, water treatment system, a 1,050-gallon polyethylene water storage tank, pressurization system, and a water service line.  A booster pump and pressure tank pressurizes the distribution system.  The water is disinfected using sodium hypochlorite solution. description: This is a proposed water system for Valles Caldera that will replace the aging non-public water system currently serving the Valle Grande area. The proposed system will include a well, treatment system, and 100,000 gallon storage tank. All details are forthcoming and subject to change.

The water system is currently classified as a non-public water system. It only has 5 active connections (ranger station, upper A frame housing unit, lower A frame housing unit, Baca Lodge housing unit, and maintenance shop) and serves about 17 staff members. The water system consists of a surface water intake, treatment building, gravity storage tank, and distribution system. The well is no longer in use and the park is utilizing a temporary surface water intake from La Jara Creek as the water source. The treatment system was originally designed for surface water source but the old infiltration gallery was destroyed due to erosion. Treatment now includes filtration (depth filters, 5 micron, 1 micron, and 1 micron absolute filters) and chlorination. Water is produced at a rate of 7 to 22 gpm, depending on how clean the filters are. Treated water is pumped to a 30,000 gallon welded steel water storage tank that is equipped with a tank mixer to keep the tank from freezing in the winter. Water flows by gravity from the water tank into the distribution system that serves buildings that are primarily used by park staff and VIPs. Future plans for visitation and usage have not been determined.

description:
This water system is classified as a Public Non-Community water system.  The system provides potable water to the visitor center, gift shop and snack bar, public restrooms, maintenance area, and residential area consisting of four houses.

Water for the park is obtained from Holloman Air Force Base (AFB).  The park taps the 16-inch AC water supply line opposite the main gate to the base on the south side of New Mexico Highway 70/82.  The system consists of a connection vault at the tap to the AFB water system, about 6.6 miles of 4-inch PVC water main installed in 2003, a treatment and controls building, an elevated water storage tank, and distribution system.  When water in the storage tank drops to a set low water level, a pressure switch located in the treatment building energizes a solenoid to open the isolation valve that connects the two water systems.  When the water level in the elevated storage tank reaches high water level, the pressure switch in the treatment building closes the isolation valve shutting off the flow to the tank.

Holloman Air Force Base, which draws water from a large well field in the Bores, San Andres, and Douglas areas, and from the City of Alamogordo, New Mexico is the source of water for the park.  The well field is located east of the AFB and approximately eight miles south of Alamogordo.  Water provided by the AFB is disinfected by a hypochlorinator with sodium hypochlorite solution.  The hypochlorinator, located in the treatment building, is energized when low water level in the storage tank turns on the pressure switch and is de-energized when the switch is turned off when high water level is detected.  The water storage tank provides adequate contact time for disinfection.  A 100,000-gallon elevated water storage tank provides storage for the park.  Constructed in the 1960‚Äôs, the tank (interior and exterior) was most recently repainted in 2019.

Park facilities located in the town of Baker include the Visitor Center, Ranger Station/Fire Cache, and staff housing.  All facilities are connected to the Baker water system.  This system includes 2 spring boxes, a treatment room with filtration, and two 50,000 gallon storage tanks.  This is the parks only year round system.

description:
This system serves the headquarters facilities, including the maintenance compound, employee housing, the visitor center, and picnic area.  It currently consists of two springs (#2, and #3), two 50,000-gallon welded steel water storage tanks, a Rosedale bag filtration system, a hypochlorinator system for disinfection, and distribution piping.  Water from spring #3, which produces about 19 gallons per minute (gpm), flows by gravity to a treatment building where it is filtered and disinfected. description:
Black Sulphur Spring is located near Rock Creek. Water flows into a concrete clearwell where it is chlorinated prior to being delivered to the single water hydrant next to the small pavilion. This spring has not been in service since 2009.

The Oklahoma Health Department has classified all springs in the park as Minor Class B (Non-Public Water Systems). This non-public classification requires that each system be tested for bacteriological quality a minimum of twice a year. DO 83 requires all non-public systems to be tested for bacteriological quality once per month.

Water is supplied to the Travertine (aka Platt District) and Bromide areas of the park from the City of Sulphur‚Äôs community water system.  The water distribution system in the park used to be classified as a Distribution System (OK3005006), but was declassified as its own public water system in April 2019.  This portion of the water system serves the Nature Center, Buffalo Springs Comfort Station, Cold Springs Campground, Rock Creek Campground, Central Campground, Bromide RV Dump Station, Maintenance Area, and 4 Housing Units.

The Buckhorn area consists of a campground with four loops, a RV dump station, a ranger station, boat launching facilities, picnic areas, a swimming beach, and five comfort stations.  The Point Area consists of a campground, boat launching facilities, a ranger station, two comfort stations, and an RV Dump Station.  A submersible pump located about 17 feet below the lake surface, pumps the water to a water treatment plant located on a hill north of the Buckhorn Area.  The water treatment plant is a rapid sand filter housed in a prefabricated steel building.  

The rapid sand filter consists of two above-grade steel tanks for chemical mixing, coagulation, sedimentation, anthracite filtration, and a clearwell.  A polymer is added to aid in coagulation/filtration and reduce the precursors for disinfection byproducts.  An ultrasonic level sensor located on the settling tank turns the submersible pump on and off based on the water level in the settling tank to run the water treatment plant in automatic mode.  The chlorinator and polymer chemical feed pumps are automatically turned on when the submersible pump is running.  The plant has the capacity to treat 114,000 gallons per day (gpd).  Winter production ranges from 2,000 to 5,000 gpd.  Summer production averages 10,000 to 15,000 gpd with a peak of over 25,000 gpd on July 4.

The finished water is chlorinated with sodium hypochlorite and flows by gravity to fill the 2 water storage tanks that are adjacent to the plant to a maximum height of 11.5 feet.  A transfer pump is also available in the water treatment plant to fill the water storage tanks to their overflow elevation.  One of the tanks is a 32,000 gallon glass-fused-to-steel tank and the other is a 25,000 gallon welded steel tank.  

The park also has a backup water source, as it is connected to the Murray County water system (OK2005012).  The systems are separated by a normally closed gate valve with a water meter so that the County can charge the park for any water used.  The water is supplied through a 3/4 ‚Äìinch diameter water meter, so flow is greatly restricted and the County water system is not capable of providing adequate water for the park during the peak water demand season (summertime).

THIS WATER SYSTEM HAS NOT BEEN ACTIVE SINCE 2020.

This system is classified by the state as a Minor B system. The Murray County Rural Water Company provides treated water and storage capacity for the Guy Sandy Area. The park does not treat or provide storage for this water. The water system operated seasonally from April to November. The Murray County Rural Water Company provides disinfection through chlorination of its water and maintains a chlorine residual of 0.4 mg/l to 0.6 mg/l in all parts of the distribution system. The Guy Sandy area is connected to the County water system via one service line.

The Headquarters Building is served by the City of Sulphur's water system and the building is maintained by the Chickasaw Nation. The building is equipped with a fire suppression system with a double check valve backflow preventer and has a fire department connection. A water softener is located in the building to soften the water. There are 2 RPZs located near the fire riser, one for the domestic water and one for the irrigation system.

Pavilion Spring is located east of Highway 177 near the Park Headquarters. A natural stone pavilion is built around the spring. Water flows from a 6-inch diameter cast-iron pipe set in a stone header in the center of the pavilion. This spring has an overflow that runs into the creek north of the spring. There is no distribution system at the site. The water is not chlorinated. Samples for bacteriological analysis are taken from the water that continually flows through the six-inch diameter cast-iron pipe. The Oklahoma Health Department has classified all springs in the park as Minor Class B (Non-Public Water Systems). This non-public classification requires that each system be tested for bacteriological quality a minimum of twice per year. DO 83 requires all non-public systems to be tested for bacteriological quality once per month.

description:
The water system at Mount Rushmore consists of two wells that are considered groundwater under the influence of surface water. They provide water through the treatment plant to a buried 500,000-gallon concrete reservoir adjacent to the plant. Within the plant the water is disinfected and treated to adjust the pH and alkalinity. Booster pumps (new in 2012) then deliver the water to two buried concrete storage reservoirs located, at the same elevation, in different areas of the park. The older 75,000-gallon reservoir is located above the maintenance shop/work area and a newer 125,000-gallon reservoir is located on a high area above the administration building. The reservoirs provide system pressure by gravity for the entire park that includes: concession restaurant, gift shop, dormitory, administration buildings, employee housing, maintenance areas, studio, visitor orientation area, public restrooms, parking lot restroom and amphitheater/visitor center.

Treated water is stored in a 500,000 gallon reservoir adjacent to the MORU WTP where it is pumped to one of two reservoirs in the park water distribution system with capacities of 75,000 and 125,000 gallons. Raw water is provided by two wells. The capacity of the oldest well is 50 gallons per minute (gpm), and the new well (2011) is 40 gpm. Peak water usage occurs in the summer months and is estimated to be 70,000 gallons per day (gpd).

The treatment process:
Groundwater is pumped through a manual strainer which removes all particles greater than 250 microns in size that could damage the membrane system. Sodium hypochlorite (not in use because arsenic is As V versus As III, hence it is already oxidized) and ferric chloride are then fed in the raw water pipe upstream of the coagulation tank for arsenic removal. The coagulation tank contains a mixer and provides the necessary detention time for floc formation to occur. Chemical storage and feed systems for sodium hypochlorite and ferric chloride were added in the new treatment building.

The turbidity of the pretreated water is monitored as the membrane filtration feed pump moves the coagulation tank effluent to the membrane system. The membrane feed pump provides the necessary pressure to force the pretreated water through membrane units. The membrane filtration system removes all materials from the water which are 0.1 micron or greater in size, which includes turbidity, bacteria, Giardia and Cryptosporidium. The membrane filtration system is maintained by backwashing and chemical cleaning. Sulfuric acid, citric acid and sodium hypochlorite storage and feed systems, including a clean-in-place tank, provide the necessary chemicals for cleaning the membranes. Compressed air is used in the monitoring and cleaning of the membranes and a compressor and air receiver provide the air needed.

Filtrate from the membrane treatment system flows into an intermediate storage tank. A filtrate booster pump supplies the pressure necessary to pump the finished water to the onsite reservoir. As the filtrate leaves the intermediate storage tank, it is monitored for turbidity on its way to pH adjustment and disinfection. Carbon dioxide and sodium hydroxide are fed to the filtrate for alkalinity adjustment and pH control, respectively. Following pH adjustment, the filtrate is disinfected with sodium hypochlorite. The hypochlorite feed is controlled manually and monitored by an oxidation / reduction (ORP) sensor. After disinfection, the finished water flows to the existing onsite storage reservoir.

Wastes from the backwashing and membrane cleaning operations, as well as tank drains, are discharged to the backwash wet well. Neutralization following maintenance washes and Clean In Place washes is performed manually in the wet well before discharge to the sewer. description:
The water system at Mount Rushmore consists of two wells that are considered groundwater under the influence of surface water. They provide water through the treatment plant to a buried 500,000-gallon concrete reservoir adjacent to the plant. Within the plant the water is disinfected and treated to adjust the pH and alkalinity. Booster pumps (new in 2012) then deliver the water to two buried concrete storage reservoirs located, at the same elevation, in different areas of the park. The older 75,000-gallon reservoir is located above the maintenance shop/work area and a newer 125,000-gallon reservoir is located on a high area above the administration building. The reservoirs provide system pressure by gravity for the entire park that includes: concession restaurant, gift shop, dormitory, administration buildings, employee housing, maintenance areas, studio, visitor orientation area, public restrooms, parking lot restroom and amphitheater/visitor center.

Treated water is stored in a 500,000 gallon reservoir adjacent to the MORU WTP where it is pumped to one of two reservoirs in the park water distribution system with capacities of 75,000 and 125,000 gallons. Raw water is provided by two wells. The capacity of the oldest well is 50 gallons per minute (gpm), and the new well (2011) is 40 gpm. Peak water usage occurs in the summer months and is estimated to be 70,000 gallons per day (gpd).

The treatment process:
Groundwater is pumped through a manual strainer which removes all particles greater than 250 microns in size that could damage the membrane system. Sodium hypochlorite (not in use because arsenic is As V versus As III, hence it is already oxidized) and ferric chloride are then fed in the raw water pipe upstream of the coagulation tank for arsenic removal. The coagulation tank contains a mixer and provides the necessary detention time for floc formation to occur. Chemical storage and feed systems for sodium hypochlorite and ferric chloride were added in the new treatment building.

The turbidity of the pretreated water is monitored as the membrane filtration feed pump moves the coagulation tank effluent to the membrane system. The membrane feed pump provides the necessary pressure to force the pretreated water through membrane units. The membrane filtration system removes all materials from the water which are 0.1 micron or greater in size, which includes turbidity, bacteria, Giardia and Cryptosporidium. The membrane filtration system is maintained by backwashing and chemical cleaning. Sulfuric acid, citric acid and sodium hypochlorite storage and feed systems, including a clean-in-place tank, provide the necessary chemicals for cleaning the membranes. Compressed air is used in the monitoring and cleaning of the membranes and a compressor and air receiver provide the air needed.

Filtrate from the membrane treatment system flows into an intermediate storage tank. A filtrate booster pump supplies the pressure necessary to pump the finished water to the onsite reservoir. As the filtrate leaves the intermediate storage tank, it is monitored for turbidity on its way to pH adjustment and disinfection. Carbon dioxide and sodium hydroxide are fed to the filtrate for alkalinity adjustment and pH control, respectively. Following pH adjustment, the filtrate is disinfected with sodium hypochlorite. The hypochlorite feed is controlled manually and monitored by an oxidation / reduction (ORP) sensor. After disinfection, the finished water flows to the existing onsite storage reservoir.

Wastes from the backwashing and membrane cleaning operations, as well as tank drains, are discharged to the backwash wet well. Neutralization following maintenance washes and Clean In Place washes is performed manually in the wet well before discharge to the sewer. The wet well contains a submersible pump which discharges through a 2 inch line to a manhole and 3 inch force main that eventually flows to the wastewater treatment plant.

description:
The contact station at Alibates Quarry (completed in 2006) is provided with water from an onsite well and pressure system. A reverse osmosis (RO) system was installed in 2013 to provide additional treatment but the system is not approved as potable by the TCEQ.  The well pumps water to a 210 gallon plastic water tank in the contact station.  The water is treated before the tank with a water softener, RO system, and pH adjustment filter.  The well pump is controlled by floats in the water tank.  Sodium hypochlorite is injected into the water tank when the well and RO system are on.   The water is then pressurized using a 100 gallon pressure tank and booster pump which are controlled by a pressure switch.  A 120 gallon chlorine contact tank is also utilized to provide chlorine contact time.  The park provides bottled water to the public and signs access points as non-potable.  

A fire suppression system consists of a ground level storage tank and booster pumps that feed a sprinkler system and outside hookup for fire hoses.  A reduced pressure zone valve assembly (RPZ) backflow device is present on the fire suppression system.  There is also a double check valve for the irrigation system and a RPZ on the plumbing in the comfort station.

description:
This Public Non-Community Transient System serves a Ranger Station, two comfort stations, a boat-launching ramp, a fish cleaning station, a RV dump station, picnic areas, and marina operated by the park.  The water source for this system is a 490-foot, 6-inch diameter well located inside the pumphouse.  A second well was drilled near the pumphouse, but remains offline.  Water from the well is chlorinated with a sodium hypochlorite and a chemical feed pump and then pumped to a 250,000-gallon concrete water tank located east of the entrance road.  Float switches in the water tank control the well pump. Operating signals are sent from the tank to the well pump via radio telemetry.  

Water from the reservoir is pressurized by a booster station located in a building adjacent to the water tank.  This booster station consists of two 10-horsepower (HP) pumps, one 5 HP booster pump, and a 250-gallon pressure tank.  The booster pumps have variable frequency drives (VFDs) that control pump operation.
source_notes: This well is also called "McNamara Well No. 2" in our files. The well is either 480 or 490 feet deep; both numbers are indicated in our files. The well is reported to have 10 feet of 8-inch casing at the surface. The remainder of the well, from 10 to 480 feet was drilled with a 7¬Ω" bit on a rotary drilling rig. The well was drilled by a firm named McNamara-Leavel and was used to furnish water for the grouting operations associated with construction of the dam.

description: This Public Non-Community Transient Water System supplies water to 7 drinking water faucets within the campground area and VIP RV site. The system consists of a 520-foot, 6-inch diameter well, a 211-gallon hydropneumatic pressure tank for storage and system pressure, and a hypochlorinator for chlorine disinfection. A pressure switch that operates the pump between 40 and 60 psi controls the well pump. A 50 micron filter cartridge is provided to remove sediment and sand. The distribution system consists of 2-inch galvanized piping that goes to the swim beach and shelter sites.

In April 2019, the park administrative staff moved into a new GSA leased facility that is now park headquarters and a visitor center.  The park has no operational responsibilities for this water system.  The water system consists of a well and pressure tank.  No information is currently available on the depth of the well and water quality testing.  The water is not chlorinated.  The park staff exceeds 25 people for more than 6 months per year, so it appears that this water system should be classified as a public water system (non-community, non-transient).  The park is currently working with GSA to have TCEQ classify the water system to establish required water testing requirements and regulatory responsibilities.

This Public Non-Community Transient Water System serves the visitor center, fish cleaning station, comfort station, ranger station, one residence, and picnic area. This employee residence is unoccupied and park administration has decided to discontinue providing employee residences at this site. Water is obtained from a 625-foot deep, 8-inch diameter well and pumped into a 20,000-gallon bolted steel reservoir located in an adjacent building. The water is chlorinated by a hypochlorinator located in the pump room prior to entering the reservoir. The well pump is controlled with float switches located in the reservoir.  The reservoir supplies a hydropneumatic pumping system that is used to maintain distribution system pressure. The pressure system, located in the pump room adjacent to the reservoir, consists of three booster pumps (3 horsepower, single PHSse) and two pressure tanks (Well-X-Trol Model WX 251). A 5 horsepower fire pump located in the pump room bypasses the pressurization system and delivers water directly from the water storage tank to the distribution. The fire pump is operated manually.
source_notes: The well is 625 feet deep. Casing (6-5/8" OD) was cemented in the upper part of the well to a depth of 151.5 feet. The remainder of the well, from 151.5 to 625 feet is uncased. From 151.5 to 625 feet the well has a diameter of 5 inches. The well obtains most of its water from solution cavities and fractures in the Devils River Limestone. The main water bearing zone is from 595 to 625 feet below ground surface. Several minor water bearing zones (less than 5 gpm) occur at shallower depths (230, 325, 410, 430 feet). Static water level in the well was approximately 153.5 feet below the top of casing at the time the well was constructed, June 9, 1980.
