The Chisos Basin (CB) water system is a Public Non-Community, Transient Water System serves the Chisos Basin Lodge and Restaurant, convenience store, Park Service and concession staff housing, picnic area and campground.

The water source consists of a spring located at Oak Springs located at the base of Chisos Mountain, outside the ‚ÄúWindow‚Äù.  The facilities include five horizontal pipes set into the spring, a concrete spring box, a concrete weir box with V-notch weir and flow recording instrument to measure flow, and overflow and bypass piping.  The flow from the spring varies considerably depending on rainfall in the recharge area.

Water is collected in a spring box and flows by gravity to a 25,000-gallon tank at Oak Springs.  Water is then transferred from the 25,000 gallon tank to a 500,000-gallon tank at Oak Springs via a small transfer pump located in an enclosure near the 25,000 gallon tank.  Two 60 horsepower booster pumps lift water from this tank at Oak Springs to a 125,000 gallon concrete tank above the basin via a dedicated water transmission line.  The water is chlorinated before entering the 125,000 gallon concrete tank with sodium hypochlorite.  Water is then filtered through a 5 micron cartridge filter followed by two filters in parallel measuring 2 microns (HC/170-LT2) to meet the requirements of the long term 2 enhanced surface water treatment rule before it is transferred to a 500,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank prior to distribution.

The Persimmon Gap (P-Gap) water system is a Public Non-Community System that serves two apartments, two VIP sites, and the visitor center. Water is hauled from the Panther Junction water system and is discharged into a 16,652 gallon bolted steel water storage tank with an aluminum roof.  The water is pressurized with two booster pumps and two pressure tanks and then water is disinfected with sodium hypochlorite, if needed, before it enters the distribution system.  A pressure switch set to operate between 40 and 60 psi pressure controls the booster pump.

This Public Community Water System serves all facilities located at Panther Junction.  This includes park and concession staff residences, maintenance yard, horse stables, Panther Junction Visitor Center, service station/convenience store, a school, K-Bar Ranch House, and the Construction Camp.

The system has 3 pressure zones and consists of three (3) producing groundwater wells, three (3) water storage tanks, two (2) booster stations, disinfection treatment systems, and a distribution system.  

Two wells with submersible pumps are located by the K-Bar Ranch House, K-Bar 5 (KB5) and K-Bar 10 (KB10).  Each well has its own pumphouse where the water is chlorinated before being discharged into a 24,000-gallon glass-fused-to-steel water storage tank constructed in 2022. These wells are operated automatically by radio telemetry based on the water level in the 24,000 gallon tank.   
   
Two 10-horsepower booster pumps, housed in a booster station building in K-Bar next to the KB-10 well pumphouse, pump water from the 24,000 gallon water storage tank to a 250,000 gallon welded steel water storage tank via a dedicated fill line.  The booster pumps are run automatically by a radio telemetry system based on the water level in the 250,000 gallon tank.  Water then flows from the 250,000 gallon tank into a 100,000 gallon concrete water tank through an altitude valve and then flows by gravity flow to the community.  A 1.5 HP booster pump and 119 gallon pressure tank located in the KB-10 pumphouse provide pressure to the K-Bar Ranch House and Construction Camp.  A recirculation line is available for this pressure zone to maintain adequate chlorine residuals in K-Bar.  Water flows by gravity to most of the facilities at Panther Junction.  

Well PJ4 is located in the staff residential area.  PJ4, pumps water through a separate pumphouse where it is chlorinated before being discharged directly into the 250,000 gallon welded storage tank.  PJ4 is run manually as needed due to its slow recharge capacity.

A booster station with booster pumps and a pressure tank is used to pressurize water for the residences at higher elevations.

The Rio Grande Village (RGV) water system serves the convenience store with shower and laundry facilities, 5 trailers, 10 houses, a trailer park, a campground with 100 sites and four comfort stations, an overflow campground area, an RV dump station, and the maintenance building.

The primary source for this system is a 798 foot deep well that was drilled in 2004 and placed into service in 2009.  The well is cased with 10-inch steel casing to a depth of 210 feet with the annual space grouted from 0 to 210 feet.  The well below 210 feet is finished in open borehole with a diameter of 6 inches.  Static water level in 2004 was 41 feet below grade.  The maximum long term sustainable well yield is estimated to be 15 gpm.  The only water quality issues with the well are secondary contaminants as follows: hardness = 720 mg/L (> 180 is considered hard), sulfates = 350 mg/L (secondary MCL = 250 mg/L), and total dissolved solids (TDS) = 670 mg/L (secondary MCL = 500 mg/L).   

Water is pumped from the well, through a treatment building where it is chlorinated, then to the 200,000 gallon glass-fused-to-steel water storage tank with an aluminum geodesic dome roof via a dedicated line.  The spring is available for backup when needed on an emergency basis only.  The spring can only be used for 24 hours per year to limit impact on the endangered gambusia pond nearby.  The spring is not equipped with filtration.  The supply line from the spring source is also routed through the treatment building for chlorination.  Control of the system is automated.

The well is located in a wash a short distance east of the tank.  The spring located about ¬Ω mile southeast of the Rio Grande Village Store.  The spring box is a stone and mortar type structure.   The water distribution system consists of 8 and 6-inch PVC water main.  The existing 8-inch ductile iron water main from the water storage tank to the distribution system was slip-lined with 6-inch PE pipe.  The treatment building contains two recirculating pumps that can circulate water from the tank (if it becomes stagnant during low water usage) and has controls for additional chlorine injection.  There is also a SCADA panel where parameters can be monitored and controlled.

A chlorine booster station building near the Berkley Cottage can inject additional chlorine into the waterline that runs to Boquillas Crossing.  This chlorine booster station has not been used to date.

This Non-Public water system serves the Barker House, a remodeled historic structure near Rio Grande Village that is used as a residence for researchers, park staff, and park guests.

An individual water well is housed in an aluminum enclosure adjacent to the residence. A 5 micron and 1 micron absolute filter are also housed in the aluminum enclosure to provide protection against giardia and cryptosporidium as the well may be under the influence of surface water.  Sodium hypochlorite is injected for disinfection followed by a 119 gallon FlexCon Mix Master chlorine contact tank with a baffling factor of 0.6 mg/L and a 80 gallon composite pressure tank to provide pressure to the house.
The Fire Complex is located in Woodville, TX and is connected to the City of Woodville municipal water system.

description:
The City of Kountze provides water to this area through approximately seven miles of six-inch water line.  Facilities served include the headquarters and maintenance building, and the visitor center.  

A separate water service line provides water to the fire suppression system for these buildings.  The fire suppression water service line is equipped with a reduced pressure zone (RPZ) backflow protection device.  The fire suppression system consists of an at-grade 75,000-gallon welded steel water storage tank and a booster station.  The water tank inlet is equipped with a float valve, which shuts off the water into the tank when the tank is full.  

Backflow devices include the double check valve for the fire suppression system at the visitor center (no longer needed), double check valve for the fire suppression system for the maintenance complex (no longer needed), the reduced pressure zone (RPZ) valve on the City water service before the fire suppression water tank, and two reduced pressure zone (RPZ) valves for the boiler system.
The Blackwell School is a single building that is served by a water service line from the City of Marfa, TX public water system (TX1890001).  The school has restrooms and an irrigation system.

The irrigation water system consists of a well, pumphouse, and water distribution system. There are several non-potable watering points located around the park to water trees and vegetation. There are two major zones of irrigation hydrants.  One zone serves the officers row area and the other serve the Historic cottonwood Grove with 12 separate hydrants.

There are several components of old potable water systems that are no longer in use, but are available for irrigation purposes.  Two wells near Building HB-1 used to supply the park with potable water before the park connected to the City‚Äôs water system. The well that was located inside the pumphouse (the pumphouse has been removed) was drilled in 1964 and a second well just outside where the pumphouse was located was drilled at a later date. A 50,000 gallon welded steel water tank constructed in 1964 is located about ¬Ω mile away from these wells. These facilities are physically disconnected from the water system.

Two wells and a pumphouse near the Church Camp used to supply the Church Camp with potable water. One well is located inside the pumphouse and another just outside the pumphouse. The Church Camp is only used for storage and the water facilities are no longer in use.

The potable water system provides water to the two park residences, the maintenance area, the Visitor Center and Administrative Offices, and Building HB1.  Water from the City enters the park through a four-inch water line with a two-inch water meter.  The water is then distributed to the park facilities via a water distribution system.  The City obtains its water from a groundwater well and disinfects the water at the source with a chlorine solution.  There is no storage or treatment of potable water within the park.  The water distribution system was replaced in 2009.

This system is classified as a Public Non-Community Transient water system (PWSID #550017).  The facilities served by this system are a campground, visitor contact station, comfort station, horse barn, a residence, and a duplex.  Water is pumped at a rate of 13 gpm from a 2,500 foot drilled well located north of the horse barn.  The water is pumped through a treatment building where it is chlorinated using sodium hypochlrorite, and then up the hill to a 54,565 gallon glass-fused-to-steel bolted water storage tank.  A pressure transducer located on the plumbing tree in the Pumphouse senses the water level in the tank an initiates well pumping cycles based on the water tank level setpoints on the control panel.  The well pump controls are currently set to start the pump when the tank level is at 15 feet and the pump is set to run for 360 minutes when started.

This water system is classified as a Public Non-Community Transient system (PWSID#: 0550015).  The facilities served by this system are a visitor contact station located at the mouth of the canyon which includes a public restroom and drinking fountain.

The source for this system is 78 foot deep well located about 500 feet north of the contact station.  The well has a pitless unit, concrete slab, and metal box used as a well cover.  Water is pumped at about 16 gpm from the well to the treatment room in the comfort station where it is passes through two cartridge filters, one 20 micron filter to remove particulates and a 0.5 micron carbon filter to remove taste and odor.  The water is then chlorinated by a hypochlorinator before being pumped into  two 300 gallon water storage tanks.  These tanks provide contact time for disinfection.  A small booster pump pressurizes two hydropneumatic tanks.  The water is distributed to the restroom facilities and drinking fountains.

This system is classified as a non-public water system.  The facilities served by this system includes a large house (Ship-of-the-Desert) with a separate apartment at one end and a small adjacent house known as the servant‚Äôs quarters.

The source for this system is a 155-foot drilled well located approximately one-half mile northwest of the house at the mouth of Lamar Canyon.  Water pumped from the well, is disinfected with sodium hypochlorite solution and treated with a roughing filter and an activated charcoal filter.  

The water then flows by gravity to a 6,000-gallon galvanized steel reservoir located between the well and the residences.  The overflow from the potable water tank flows into two open stone tanks used for water storage in the event of fire fighting activities.  Water from the potable tank is then distributed to the house via 2-inch galvanized iron pipe.  There is a water softener and reverse osmosis treatment system installed at the facility that is not used.

This water system is classified as a Public Community water system (PWSID #55014).  The system provides potable water to the Visitor Center and administrative offices, the maintenance area and residential area for park employees (consisting of 12 houses, four duplex units, two apartment units, and a recreation center), a campground and comfort station located at Pine Springs about one mile north of the Visitor Center, and the ranch house, horse corral, and storage buildings at Frijole Spring.  The system also provides water to the Texas Highway Department that has six houses, maintenance building, and an office located adjacent to the park maintenance area.

The water source for this system is the Glover Well Number 13, a 2,572-foot, 8-inch diameter drilled well located in the center of the parking area in front of the Pine Springs comfort station.  The pumping rate for the well is about 52 gpm.  The well is cased with 8-inch steel casing to 2,502 feet, and open hole to the bottom with the pump is set at approximately 2,480 feet. The well pump is operated manually to fill the reservoir.  A sensor in the reservoir automatically de-energizes the pump.  An emergency power generator is available to power the system in the event of a power outage.

The water is pumped from the well through a treatment room in the comfort station.  In the treatment room the water is first filtered through a multimedia filter (charcoal and sand/gravel) to remove iron bacteria and other particulates, as well as taste and odor caused by VOC‚Äôs from the raw well water.  The water is then injected with Aqua Mag, an iron sequestering chemical, and sodium hypochlorite for disinfection.  The filter is manually backwashed with the backwash water being discharged into the comfort station septic system.  

After treatment, the water then enters a 218,000-gallon, two-compartment, below-grade concrete reservoir approximately 1,000 feet up the Canyon.  Water flows out of the reservoir through a distribution system consisting largely of 8 and 6-inch PVC water main.  A booster pump located in the comfort station pressurizes water for use in the comfort station.  A pressure reducing valve (PRV) located by the highway reduces the water pressure to the maintenance area  and a second PRV reduces the pressure again to residences located to the east of the maintenance building.

The Fritch Fortress distribution system is considered part of the Sanford Yake public water system by the state of Texas.  This system serves an RV dump station, comfort station, and the amphitheater.  The Fritch Fortress water system is connected to the City of Fritch Water System.  The point of connection is housed in a concrete building.  The plumbing tree includes a pressure reducer, which reduces the incoming pressure from 100 psi to 60 psi, and a hypochlorinator.  This system is used only during the peak season and is shut down the rest of the time.  The system is flushed and tested for bacteriological contamination before the season begins.  The City of Fritch Water Department chlorinates the water before it is delivered to Fritch Fortress.  Supplemental chlorination facilities are provided at the point of connection but are seldom used.  Adequate volume and pressure for the Fritch Fortress system is provided by the City of Fritch Water department, therefore an existing 100,000-gallon elevated water storage tank is not in service.  It has been completely disconnected from the water system.

This Public Non-Community Transient serves an RV dump station, Marina Store and comfort station, Marina boat pump-out station, Sanford Yake comfort station, and Cedar Canyon comfort station. Water is supplied from the Fritch Municipal Water Supply (TX1170004).  The municipal system disinfects the water before entering the Sanford Yake storage and distribution system.  Water is distributed from the water storage tank to the RV dump station, Sanford Yake comfort station, Cedar Canyon comfort station, Marina store and comfort station, and the maintenance/ranger complex.

The park has the capability of providing additional disinfection, but does not routinely do so.  Storage for the Sanford Yake distribution system consists of a 100,000-gallon elevated water storage tank.  Separate inlet and outlet pipes are provided to assure circulation throughout the tank and to provide adequate contact time for disinfection.

description: This Public Non-Community Transient water system (PWS#0860008) serves an office with a sink and a comfort station with drinking fountain. The system consists of a drilled well and hypochlorinator housed in a separate enclosure, a 500-gallon plastic water storage tank, and pressurization system located in a small building. Water is pumped from the well by a submersible pump, disinfected with sodium hypochlorite solution, and discharged into the water storage tank. The tank provides storage and chlorine contact time. The water is pressurized with a booster pump and two bladder-type hydropneumatic tanks before entering the distribution piping. There is a separate irrigation system consisting of a well, pressure tank and distribution piping. The pressure tank is located in the same building as the tanks for the potable water. The 6-inch diameter, 200 foot deep drilled well is located approximately 450 feet northeast of the house. The well has a casing and sanitary seal depth of 50 feet, a yield of 7 gpm, and a static water level of 18 feet. The 2 horsepower pump is set at 137 feet.

description: This area of the park is connected to the Johnson City community water system. This area consists of the Park Headquarters and visitor center, education center, Jones House, Cantwell House, Walker House, Boyhood Home comfort station, the Settlement Exhibit Center comfort station. The sources for the system are groundwater wells owned and operated by Johnson City located outside Park boundaries. The City also provides all necessary treatment (chlorination) and storage. There are approximately 11 wells identified within the Park boundary that have been sealed as required by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ). There are three wells at the Boyhood Home site. The first is a shallow drilled well behind the house used for irrigation. A second drilled well located adjacent to the irrigation well was not in use and has been sealed. The third well is a dug well in front of the house. It has a rock casing extending above the ground that is enclosed with a wooden cover. The well is 4 feet 4 inches in diameter and is 41¬Ω feet deep. The well has been filled with sand to prevent the accumulation of water.  There are two interpretive wells at the Settlement. One is a dug well in front of the Sam Ealy Johnson Log Cabin and the other is a drilled well equipped with a windmill used to supply a tank and provide water to the Cooling House located on the north edge of the settlement. Neither of these wells is used as a source of drinking water. There are five backflow prevention assemblies within the park headquarters area. One reduced pressure zone assembly valve (RPZ) is used to protect the potable water from the water used for the chiller tower and another RPZ protects the potable water system from the boiler. A double check valve backflow assembly provides protection from backflow from the VC fire sprinkler system. There are also double check valves on the Education Center and Cantwell House fire systems.

description:
This Public Non-Community Transient (PWS # 0860084) system serves the LBJ Ranch House, Ranch buildings, Klein‚Äôs shop, Malechek House, Bus Barn, Show Barn, and four Ranch VIP RV trailer sites. Water is used at the Show Barn for a restroom and cattle washing, and at the Bus Barn for two restrooms and drinking fountains. A drinking water fountain is provided for the public at the Show Barn. Water is pumped from the Martin well through a water treatment building where it is disinfected with sodium hypochlorite solution. From the treatment building the water is pumped to two 55,000 gallon glass-fused-to-steel bolted water storage tanks via a dedicated fill line. A float switch located in one of the tanks senses pump-on and pump-off water levels. This information is transmitted to the well pumphouse by a buried control cable, which then controls well pump operation. Water flows out of the steel tanks by gravity when demanded via a water distribution system consisting of 10-inch cast iron pipe. 

 Isolation valves on the bolted steel tanks allow one of the tanks to be removed from service while the other remains online. A gauge mounted on the outside of the bolted steel tank is used to determine water level in the tanks. A diesel operated fire pump remains in place but is no longer connected to the system.  Fire hydrants located throughout the distribution system provide fire protection to the Ranch buildings.  There is a pressure system installed in the same building as the fire pumps that provides pressure to the Malechek House, Showbarn, and VIP sites.  The pressure system consist of a 5 HP booster pump, 2 pressure tanks, and a pressure switch.  A separate pressure system for the Bus Barn consists of a small booster pump, pressure tank, and pressure switch is located in a small above ground enclosure near the Bus Barn.

The backup water sources for this system are the North and South Wells.  Both wells are piped into a pumphouse located near the Texas White House.  The South Well is currently offline.  A float located in a 525 gallon PE water storage tank initiates well pumping cycles.  The water is chlorinated before entering the tank using sodium hypochlorite and a chemical feed pump.  Water is then pressurized by a 1 HP booster pump and 2 pressure tanks that are controlled by a pressure switch.  The North and South Wells and pumphouse are used for irrigation and are physically disconnected from the potable water system in the pumphouse.  A PVC cap located behind the pressure tanks can be removed and a compression coupling can be connected in order to connect these wells into the potable water system if needed.

There are two water systems at Capitol Reef National Park.  The first system is an irrigation that is fed off of a diversion of the Fremont River.  This system is completely separated from the potable water system.  The other system is a potable water system fed by a solar powered well pump.  The well is approximately 80 feet deep and has a 6" casing insided of a 12" casing with the void between filled with grout.  Within the well are two pumps; the solar powered pump can provide 2-50 GPM depending upon available sunlight; the other pump is powered by a generator and can be used in emergency situations.  After leaving the well the water flows to the treatment building and into three platic 300 gallon tanks operated in parallel.  The water is then transferred to the RO skid where it is pressurized with a pump and flows through a water softener.  The water then flows through one of two 5 micron cartidge filters and carbon filters operated in parralel, then through a VFD pump into the RO filters.  After exiting the RO skid the water has liquid sodium hypochlorite injected into the water and flows into the clear well.  The clear well has a float control and when needed will pump water to the buried 100,000 gallon concrete storage tank.  From the storage tank water will flow into the Park's distribution system.

description: The UVU field station is supplied by a drilled well that has been deemed GWUDI due to a short seal on the well.  Water is received from the well to the treatment building where it flows through a sand separator into a 1000 gallon settling tank (also necessary to provide consistent flow to the filtration units).  It is then pumped through an iron-neutralizing tank with oxygen injected into the water.  From that tank if flows to a sediment collection tank to 3 cartridge filters operated in parallel through a check valve.  After the check valve, the water flows to a black polyethylene reaction tank, then through two nanofilters operated in parallel.  After the nanofilters, it is treated with a GE Homespring microfiltration unit, chlorinated and then the water flows through a check valve to a distribution pump and into four 119 gallon pressure tanks.

description: The water system comes from Blow Hard spring to a spring box.  In the spring box, water flows through a wire mesh filter to the pump house through a 1,800 foot PVC line.  In the pump house, water goes into a 3,500 gallon clearwell, excess water flows through a screened overflow tube into the nearby valley.  In the pumphouse liquid chlorine is injected into the tank as water is pumped through a polyethylene transmission line to a two cell buried 150,000 gallon storage tank. From the reservoirs the distribution system is fed by gravity.  The distribution system is composed of PVC and ductile iron pipe.

The Green River Campground has a Transient Non-Community Water system that services 4 comfort stations, VIP sites and a seasonal ranger residence.  Water comes from a drilled well that is disinfected with liquid sodium hypochlorite and is transmitted to a 20,000 gallon storage tank.  From the storage tank water is distributed to the comfort stations, VIP sites and the ranger residence.

The Quarry water system is a distribution system that is supplied by the Jensen Water Improvement District (PWSID UTAH24010).  The system serves residences, a maintenance area, administrative offices,  a visitor center and limited distribution to the Quarry building (the Quarry building is temporarily closed due to being structurally unsound).  Water is received tharough a 4 inch PVC line and liquid sodium hypochlorite is injected into the water to boost the level in the water that is received. This transient, non-community water system serves the Hite area of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area ‚Äì including the campground, staff housing, gas station and store, and maintenance facility. A 400-foot drilled well, classified as ground water under the direct influence due to the location adjacent to the Colorado River), serves this water system. Water is pumped through a submersible pump to an outdoor concrete settling basin reservoir, installed during 2011. Water exits this settling basin and is pumped into a  Pall Aria Water Treatment System, installed during 2020. After entering this system, water undergoes prefiltration through a 400-micron prefilter and a 0.1-micron membrane. Following filtration, water travels into a 4,500-gallon bright tank. Following the bright tank, water undergoes filtration through a 5-micron filter prior to reverse osmosis treatment through a GE Osmonics Muni Series Reverse Osmosis (RO) unit. Caustic soda ash is added to the RO unit to adjust the pH. Water undergoes through two stages of membrane filtration prior to treatment injection utilizing a liquid sodium hypochlorite solution. Treated water undergoes chlorine detention inside a 4,000-gallon clearwell. Once the detention time is met, potable water travels through a 3-inch water line for storage inside two, 25,000-gallon buried fiberglass potable water storage reservoirs. Potable water is sent from these two, 25,000-gallon potable water storage reservoirs for distribution throughout this area of the Park. Additionally, two, 50,000-gallon buried fiberglass potable water storage reservoirs are located in the Park housing area to provide for additional storage.

The source for this transient, non-community water system is a 280-foot deep drilled well. Water from the well is pumped into the water treatment building through a submersible pump. Water from this well is high in sediment concentration, so it passes through a strainer prior to undergoing filtration through a 5-micron cellulose cartridge filter. Following filtration, sodium hypochlorite solution is injected through an 85 MD17 Stenner pump. After treatment, potable water is stored inside a 1,500-gallon above ground potable water storage reservoir to achieve the appropriate chlorine contact time. Potable water travels from the reservoir back into the water treatment building and is pressurized using 2 Hydropro model # V250D pressure tanks and booster pumps. Following pressurization, potable water is sent for distribution, where the line splits in two directions. A Watts 919-QT reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assembly backflow prevention device is attached to the water line serving the truck filling station. The other water line sends potable water for distribution throughout the Lone Rock area of the Park.

The visitor center system is pressurized by using hydropneumatic tanks.  Afire pump is located near the locomotive shed. description: This Public Transient Non-Community System serves the visitor center that has three restrooms and 1 outside faucet, the ranger housing area that consists of 9 year-round residences, and administrative offices.  This system serves all of the facilities in the park.  The water system consists of 2 ground water wells, a pumphouse with liquid sodium hypochlorite system, a 50,000 gallon above ground water storage tank, and a booster system with two 3 HP booster pumps and two 264 gallon pressure tanks.  Well #3, constructed in 1979, is 750 feet deep with perforations from 270-280 feet and 539-689 feet and is equipped with a 3 HP submersible well pump that pumps approximately 3 gpm.  Well #3 is only run seasonally, since a portion of the water main from Well #3 to the pumphouse is above grade due to rock and is subject to freezing. Aqua-Mag was injected as a sequestering agent to improve water quality, but has been offline since 2007.

description:
The majority of users in the Park are served by a community water system comprised of four springs: Birch Creek and Watercress Spring and the Upper and Lower Grotto Spring. The Wylie Spring has been taken off-line due to damage from a rock slide.

The Birch (105 GPM) and Watercress (40 GPM) springs typically serve the area from the mule corrals down.  Water is collected from both springs and runs to individual concrete 3 chamber settling weirs to allow for the sand to separate from the water.  After the settling chambers the water is combined and injected with liquid sodium hypochlorite.  Water is then stored in a 1,000,000 gallon storage tank.  From the storage tank, water flows to a hydropneumatic tank for increased water pressure then to the distribution system. A Baldor 140 GPM pump is available to send water from the 1,000,000 gallon storage tank to the Grotto 300,000 gallon storage tank as needed.

The upper canyon is served with water from the Upper Grotto.  The Upper Grotto (60 GPM) produces water that flows to a 3 chamber sand trap to a 5 micron cartridge filter and 1 micron bag filter and then is injected with liquid sodium hypochlorite. The Lower Grotto produces water at 60 GPM that flows to a sand trap (a 5,000 gallon storage tank) to a 5 micron cartridge filter then a 1 micron bag filter and then is injected with liquid sodium hypochlorite.  After chlorine injection, the water from both the Upper and Lower Grotto is combined and piped to a 300,000 gallon storage tank.

This system consists of a outdoor well with a submersible pump and a sanitary well cap. The well casing is raised above ground just over two feet with a concrete apron. There is a well log available. The well was completed February 1, 2012. It was screened in unconsolidated soil (sand and clay). It is 410 ft deep, cased to 385 ft, and grouted to 100 ft. The well is activated by an in-line pressure switch. Water storage tank levels are controlled by pressure switches. Water is called for when the tank level dropped to a preset level (94.5 ft), this activates the reverse osmosis (RO) unit (GE E4 Osmonics) and booster pump. Water is pumped from the well, passes through a meter, sand filter, two pressure tanks, water softener, silica filter, and a RO unit after which Aqua Mag blended phosphate solution is injected followed by sodium hypochlorite solution (chemical feed pumps were Stenner Model 45MHP22). The system serves the entire park: visitor center, colonial kitchen, spinning and weaving shop, craft shop, log house conference center, picnic area restrooms, maintenance building, water treatment plant and Quarters #1 and #2. description: The domestic water system consists of two 8‚Äù diameter screened wells, two well pumps equipped with adjustable speed controllers, two hypochlorination systems with an inline static mixer, a pipe loop contactor, a small pressure tank, and a distribution system with all the necessary valving. The domestic well pumps were replaced in 2012 and are dual voltage submersible vertical turbine pumps. Design criteria was based on 100 gpm flow capacity at a TDH of 144 feet.  Each well pump is also equipped with an adjustable speed pump controller, connected to a pressure transducer located at the outlet to the distribution system, so that pumps operate in a multi-pump lead-lag configuration to maintain a constant distribution system pressure of 62 psi. An 81-gallon pressure tank provides small drawdown capacities on drive start-up and provides a ‚Äúcushion‚Äù for the entire system at normal operation (and provides compressibility upon shut-down). The nominal 14-inch high density polyethylene (HDPE) DR17 pipe loop contactor was designed and installed to provide plug-flow conditions. The pipe loop system length distributed on a set of support racks totals almost 171 feet in length. A step-dose tracer test was conducted in March 2019 to verify the geometry and baffling of the pipe loop contactor and to document contact time (T) at various flows. At a peak flow rate of 140 gpm, disinfectant contact time is 8.1 minutes and requires a minimum free chlorine residual of 0.74 mg/L. A third supplemental well provides unchlorinated water for fire protection purposes. The supplemental well system consists of a well and pump, pressure sensor, flow meter with double check valve, and fire hydrant with a sampling station. Both the domestic wells and the (unchlorinated) supplemental well utilize the same pipe distribution system. DOH does not require a certified operator for this system.

description:
This system consists of a spring source that flows by gravity to the treatment building for filtration through a 50 micron cartridge prefilter, a 5 micron intermediate cartridge filter, and a bag filter system.  After continuous disinfection, the treated water flows to a polyethylene water

This year-round non-community system consists of a 100-foot-deep well, submersible pump, continuous disinfection, and hydropneumatic pressure tanks. Due to elevated turbidity, color, and iron content, raw water is passed through a 5 micron bag filter to remove iron particulate prior to disinfection, and orthophosphate is fed continuously to reduce the effects of iron (i.e. staining of fixtures) on the system. In 2018, the water treatment process was relocated to a new precast concrete water treatment building with new water treatment equipment. In 2019, the park replaced all 1‚Äù and 2‚Äù PVC distribution piping with 2‚Äù HDPE pipe, plus installed a new 130 linear foot section of in-ground 12‚Äù HDPE pipe for increased disinfection contact time. The current submersible well pump, which was installed in December 2017 to replace in-kind the previous pump, is a three-wire 0.5 HP Franklin Electric 10FV05P4-3W230 series V submersible pump set at a depth of 91 feet that provides approximately 13 GPM under 110 feet of total dynamic head. The well pump provides pressure for the treatment process, which consists of a 5 micron bag style filter that removes iron particulate immediately upon entering the treatment building. A second 1 micron final filter was added in series following the initial 5 micron pre-filter; Strainrite‚Äôs AquaRite Vessels (model AQ2-2F) are coupled with AquaRite Prefilter & Filter Bags (SWT1-P2S-8T & HPM97-GC-2SS), and differential pressure of 25 psid is used to determine the need for filter exchange. Filtered water is injected with Aqua Mag blended phosphate (8 oz per gallon of water) to sequester unfiltered iron and reduce discoloration and staining associated with finished water. After filtration and sequestration, water is disinfected with a 12.5% sodium hypochlorite solution (100 mL per gallon of water). Chemical feed pumps are controlled through a switched outlet so they are energized when the well pump is initiated to prevent chemical overfeed. Two 120-gallon pressurized well tanks located inside the treatment building maintain approximately 40 psi pressure throughout the distribution system. DOH requires a certified WTPO1 to operate this system.

Whitman Mission water system (ID #NP980) is a group A, transient, non-community public water system. Water source is a deep well drilled in September 1961 and the well head is housed in a dedicated room in the Utility building. The well was completed with 12-inch steel casing to 524 foot depth and open borehole from 524 feet to 755 feet. Silt and clay layers were encountered in the borehole from 15 ft to 517 ft, providing a highly effectively seal of the water bearing formation. The water bearing formation is the Frenchman Springs Member of the Wanapum Basalt, a member of the Columbia River Basalt Group. At the well location, this formation appears from 517 feet to 755 feet and static water level at well completion was 35 ft. The well yield was recorded as 77 gallons per minute with draw down of 310 feet.  

A five horse-power submersible pump was sized to pump at 29 GPM and installed at 342 foot depth.  In 2014, the park added 105 feet to the depth of the pump due to air entering the line during extended run times.  The pump depth is now 447 feet.  A wellhead assessment was completed in 2014 to ensure no impact from site conditions and fuel tank.  Water is chlorinated and pumped to a 50,000 gallon cast-in-place concrete tank which is located approximately 1100 feet east of the well head and 100 feet above in elevation.  The water system services the Park Visitor Center and administrative office, a single family residence, Park Utility Building, and three drinking fountains during the summer.  

The water system also irrigates approximately 3.5 acres of lawn from April through October. Water production averages 10,800 gallons per day in the summer and 900 gallons per day in the winter. Potable use averages 500 gallons per day in the months of May through October and 300 gallons per day in the months of November through April. The majority of summer consumption goes to irrigation of lawn which has been replaced with native grasses with the expectation of water demand to decrease significantly once the grass is established.

description:

IN 2022, THIS WATER SYSTEM WAS MOVED TO JODR.

description: Drinking water for this water system is supplied by two groundwater wells that are located directly adjacent to the treatment building.  Water is pumped directly from the wells to the treatment building constructed in 2018 where it is chlorinated with liquid sodium hypochlorite.  Sodium bicarbonate can be added for alkalinity control due to historic lead and copper problems on the system, but the water is only slightly corrosive and the old plumbing has been replaced in all of the residences, so the sodium bicarbonate is not currently used.  There is a back-up generator located next to the treatment building.  Following chlorination, the water is pumped to a new 300,000 gallon buried concrete water tank constructed in 2018.  The water system serves Moose and Beaver Creek.

The park acquired the Moulton Cabins in 2019 from a private inholding.  The water system provides water to the main house, bathhouse, and a kitchenette.  The 8 cabins in this location have no water service, as they use the shared bathhouse and kitchenette.  The water system consists of a drilled well with 2 EA WellXtrol WX451C (158 gallons/each) bladder type pressure tanks located in the basement of the main house.  The well pump cycle is initiated based on the pressure switch settings (30/50 psi) to pressurize the pressure tanks.  The main house has an antifreeze type wet fire suppression system with a reduced pressure zone (RPZ) backflow prevention device that serves the main house, grand cabin, bunk house, and cabin 3.  The water system also has an irrigation system with a double check valve backflow protection device.

The well pump is controlled by floats in the reservoir and the system is connected to the parkwide SCADA monitoring system.  There is a continuous chlorine analyzer with digital readout in the treatment building.  

Storage:  After disinfection the treated water is pumped to two buried 50,000 gallon fiberglass storage tanks via a dedicated fill line.

Distribution:  An 8" fire main line supplies a fire pump and fire hydrants.  A 4" distribution main supplies domestic use.  Two jockey pumps and a pressure tank maintain pressure in the domestic distribution system.  The distribution main downstream of the pressure pumps is a 6" line.

This non-public water system serves a historic ranch that is currently undergoing extensive rehabilitation and will eventually serve as the Western Center for Historic Preservation, a public-private partnership project of the National Trust and National Park Service.  The system consists of a well, a chlorine treatment building that also houses a 500 gallon hydropneumatic tank for storage and distribution pressure.  The well was drilled in 2004 to a total depth of 98 feet and was completed with perforated casing from 75-90 feet. The well was test pumped at 50 gpm for 24 hours, resulting in 30 feet of drawdown.
